items.title: Jahrespressekonferenz jetzt auf YouTube

_analysis.plain_english_type: Press release from a competition authority
_analysis.summary: The Bundeskartellamt (Germany's competition authority) announced that its annual press conference will now be livestreamed on YouTube, highlighting the use of a major digital platform for public communication. This reflects the authority's engagement with digital tools in its outreach.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this shows a competition authority adapting to digital communication, it does not directly address market power or competition issues.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals the increasing role of digital platforms like YouTube in institutional communication, though not directly tied to competition dynamics.

items.title: FinRank: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Financial Question Answering and Retrieval over SEC Filings
items.abstract: Financial question answering is typically evaluated by answer correctness, yet in SEC filings a plausible and even numerically correct answer can be grounded in the wrong evidence. Similar facts and disclosures recur across sections of a filing, across reporting periods of the same firm, and across comparable firms. FinRank targets this provenance-sensitive retrieval problem by requiring systems to identify evidence for the intended entity, reporting period, and disclosure context. The benchmark contains 1185 manually authored question-answer records over the 10-K and 10-Q filings of 22 companies. Each record includes a reference answer, gold supporting passages, and hand-curated hard negatives drawn from confusable passages within filings, across reporting periods, and across comparable firms. FinRank evaluates passage retrieval, reranking, and hard-negative discrimination as separately measured tasks. Baseline results demonstrate the difficulty of this setting: among the evaluated systems, even a 7B instruction-tuned embedder reaches only 44.8% Recall@10 on the pooled evidence corpus; sub-billion-parameter encoders gain at most 3.5 points over BM25, a finance-adapted embedder tra

_analysis.summary: FinRank introduces a new benchmark for evaluating financial question-answering systems over SEC filings (10-K and 10-Q documents), focusing on 'provenance-sensitive retrieval'—ensuring answers are grounded in the correct evidence, context, and reporting period. The benchmark includes 1,185 manually created question-answer pairs across 22 companies, addressing the challenge of verifying numerical or plausible answers in complex, repetitive financial disclosures.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper highlights the importance of accurate, traceable information retrieval in financial markets, which is critical for transparency and could influence how regulators assess data access and verification in digital platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of AI-driven financial analysis tools may increase demand for high-quality, verifiable data sources, potentially reshaping how investors and regulators access and trust financial information.

items.title: Revealed Default Under Choice Overload
items.abstract: Empirical and experimental studies suggest that a decision maker frequently remains with their default option when making choices even when more preferred alternatives are available, yet standard choice data may not record which option is the default. Existing default-based models often assume that the default option is observed. In contrast, I study a decision maker subject to status quo bias and choice overload and illustrate how one can identify both the decision maker's default and preference from the observed behavior. This paper shows that anomalous choice behavior may arise from a latent default, a possibility largely overlooked in studies of standard choice data.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how people often stick with their default option when faced with too many choices (a phenomenon called 'status quo bias' and 'choice overload'). It proposes a method to identify both the default option and a person's true preferences from their observed behavior, even when the default isn't explicitly recorded.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Understanding default behavior and choice overload is crucial for analyzing how digital platforms (like app stores or recommendation systems) steer users toward certain options, which can influence market power and consumer harm.
_analysis.market_signal: This research signals that digital platforms may exploit default settings and choice overload to shape user behavior, potentially reinforcing market dominance.

items.title: Reading Copom's Tone: A Weighted LLM Framework for Hawkish-Dovish Sentiment, Forward Guidance, and Uncertainty
items.abstract: This paper documents an applied natural-language-processing framework for measuring the tone of Brazilian Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) statements. The project is explicitly inspired by iSent, Itaú's Central Bank sentiment classifier, particularly its sentence-level division of official communication into hawkish, dovish, neutral, and out-of-context classes. The implementation extends that idea in three directions. First, an LLM identifies short hawkish and dovish expressions and assigns each a 0-to-1 intensity weight. Second, the document index combines sentence counts with document-specific average signal intensities, producing a bounded score from -1 to 1. Third, a separate full-document layer measures forward-guidance direction, guidance explicitness, uncertainty level, and change in uncertainty. The empirical sample is restricted to communications dated August 2016 or later and contains 80 statements and 1,498 classified sentences from August 31, 2016 through August 5, 2026. Across this sample, 33.3% of sentences are hawkish, 18.0% dovish, 42.1% neutral, and 6.5% out of context. The average document score is +0.107, while the most hawkish reading is +0.570 in August 2021.

_analysis.summary: This paper presents a natural-language-processing (NLP) framework using large language models (LLMs) to analyze the tone of monetary policy statements from Brazil’s Central Bank (Copom). It classifies statements as hawkish (favoring tighter monetary policy), dovish (favoring looser policy), neutral, or out-of-context, assigning intensity weights to expressions. The tool builds on Itaú’s iSent classifier but extends it with LLM-based sentence-level analysis.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on monetary policy, the LLM-based sentiment analysis framework signals the growing use of advanced AI tools for regulatory and market monitoring, which could indirectly influence digital competition policy by improving transparency in platform communications or algorithmic decision-making.
_analysis.market_signal: The adoption of LLM-driven sentiment analysis tools in regulatory contexts may accelerate the use of AI for monitoring digital platform behavior, potentially aiding antitrust enforcement or market oversight.

items.title: Measuring Concept Content in Text from LLM Activations: ESG Evidence from Concept Vectors and Linear Probes
items.abstract: Existing measures of how much a text is about a concept read the surface of the text: dictionary word shares, topic proportions, embedding similarities. They score the words a text uses, not the judgment a reader forms about it. Recent work has shown that a gap exists in what Large Language Models (LLMs) know internally versus what they express in their response. This paper asks whether that internal knowledge, read by monitoring the activations of frozen, out-of-the-box LLMs, can stand in for task-specific fine-tuning when measuring concept content, and which extraction method reads it best. We extract such measures via the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm and via linear probing, and compare these against an embedding baseline, surface baselines, and the same model's own answer to the question. We demonstrate the approach on financial text, a domain studied extensively and served by established annotated resources, using a human-annotated Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) dataset. The best linear probe comes within 0.6 percentage points of a fine-tuned domain classifier's accuracy without any task-specific fine-tuning, and outscores the same model's own answer to

_analysis.summary: This paper explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can reveal their internal understanding of concepts—like Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) topics—by analyzing their internal activations (the signals processed during text generation) rather than just their output. It compares methods like 'concept vectors' and 'linear probes' to extract this hidden knowledge from frozen (untrained) LLMs, suggesting these techniques could measure concept content more accurately than traditional text-based methods.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work highlights how LLMs encode and process conceptual knowledge internally, which could inform debates about transparency, explainability, and potential biases in AI systems—key concerns for digital competition policy.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in interpreting LLM activations may accelerate the development of AI systems that can autonomously analyze or generate content, potentially disrupting markets reliant on human-curated data or intermediation.

items.title: Auditing Algorithmic Collusion from Strategy Graphs
items.abstract: Detecting algorithmic collusion is challenging because regulators often have limited access to firms' algorithms, training data, and market information. We study an intermediate-information regime in which an auditor can query firms' frozen pricing policies and construct the induced strategy graph. Using a complete characterization of Nash equilibria in a repeated pricing game, we identify graph-theoretic features of strategy graphs that are associated with collusive reward-and-punishment schemes, including maximum betweenness, attractor in-degree, and average path length. We then test these metrics on policies learned by decentralized Q-learning and the Q-learning algorithm of Calvano et al. (2020). We find that especially the maximum betweenness and attractor in-degree are strongly correlated with the standard profit-based Collusion Index. Importantly, the proposed metrics rely only on the unlabeled topology of strategy graphs and require neither price histories, demand estimates, nor competitive and monopoly benchmarks. Our results suggest that the structure of frozen pricing policies contains robust signals of collusion among reinforcement learning algorithms and provides a pro

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a method to detect potential collusion between AI pricing algorithms by analyzing the 'strategy graphs' they create—visual representations of how algorithms react to different market conditions. The authors identify specific graph features (like 'maximum betweenness' and 'attractor in-degree') that may indicate collusive behavior, even when regulators lack full access to firms' algorithms or data.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Provides a practical framework for regulators to audit algorithmic pricing systems for collusion, directly informing enforcement under antitrust laws like the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA).
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that AI-driven pricing algorithms could enable tacit collusion, potentially undermining competitive markets and requiring proactive regulatory oversight.

items.title: Acceptant Expansions of Path-Independent Choice Rules
items.abstract: A choice rule is $q$-acceptant if it chooses $\min\{q,|X|\}$ alternatives from each set $X$. We show that a path-independent rule of maximum cardinality at most $q$ need not have a $q$-acceptant path-independent expansion, refuting Chambers and Yenmez (2017, Theorem 4). We construct a one-school matching market whose unique stable matching leaves a seat vacant that no path-independent expansion of the school's rule fills. Every path-independent rule satisfying the law of aggregate demand has such an expansion. We characterize the choice rules admitting an acceptant expansion by monotone selections of rejected alternatives.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines 'q-acceptant' choice rules—rules that select a fixed number of alternatives (up to q) from any set—and challenges prior findings by showing that not all path-independent rules (rules where choices depend only on the final set, not the selection process) can be expanded into q-acceptant rules. It demonstrates this with a one-school matching market example where a stable matching leaves a seat empty, and no path-independent expansion can fill it. The paper also characterizes which choice rules can admit such expansions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on abstract choice theory and matching markets, its insights into path-independent rules and expansions could indirectly inform discussions on algorithmic decision-making in digital platforms, particularly in areas like ad auctions or recommendation systems.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the complexity of designing fair and stable algorithmic selection mechanisms in digital markets, highlighting potential gaps in current approaches to preference aggregation.

items.title: Linguistic Pattern Based Optimization of Economic and Spatial Uniformity Criteria in Facility Layout Problems
items.abstract: This paper extends prior work on linguistic pattern based facility layout optimization by enhancing the LP Alinks framework with an explicit spatial uniformity criterion. While earlier studies demonstrated that linguistic patterns can effectively encode expert knowledge and guide agent based layout emergence, their optimization scope remained limited to cost oriented objectives. To address this gap, we introduce the Normalized Coverage Score (NCS), a scale adjusted measure of spatial evenness that complements the classical flow distance economic objective and enables systematic exploration of cost uniformity trade offs. A full factorial experiment comprising 324 conditions evaluates the combined effects of problem size, link density, virtual force scaling, and two families of membership functions on both objectives. Five way and nested three way ANOVAs reveal that structural factors (number of objects and link density) exert a dominant baseline influence on both economic performance and spatial uniformity. However, while economic cost is overwhelmingly governed by these structural characteristics, uniformity is substantially more sensitive to the linguistic pattern parameters, whic

_analysis.summary: This academic paper improves a method for optimizing the layout of facilities (like warehouses or stores) by adding a new measure called the Normalized Coverage Score (NCS) to ensure spatial evenness. The work builds on prior research that used linguistic patterns (structured human knowledge) to guide automated layout design, but previously only focused on cost efficiency rather than balanced spatial distribution.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on physical facility layouts, its methodology for balancing economic and spatial objectives could inspire similar approaches in digital platform design, such as optimizing ad placement or content recommendation systems.
_analysis.market_signal: This research signals a growing trend in using structured optimization techniques to balance multiple objectives in system design, which may influence how digital platforms balance efficiency and fairness in their algorithms.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models and the Unity of Economic Behaviour
items.abstract: Economics uses different behavioural models for risk, time, losses, valuation, and social choice. I study a unified choice experiment in which the same decision makers face all these domains. I hide a decision maker's choices in one domain and ask a frozen tabular foundation model to recover them from that decision maker's choices elsewhere and labelled choices by other participants. The foundation model improves on the training-sample median, and the gain disappears when visible choices are shuffled across decision makers. I then estimate one random-utility model over the foundation model's learned representation. This structural model applies the same utility function in every domain, retains most of the foundation model's reduction in prediction error, predicts domains excluded from utility estimation, and reproduces how behavioural measures co-move across people. The resulting model separates three objects: a learned common choice domain, one systematic utility function on that domain, and one random component that generates stochastic choice on observed menus.

_analysis.summary: This paper explores whether a single 'tabular foundation model' (a type of AI trained on structured data) can predict human economic behavior across different domains like risk, time, losses, and social choice. The study finds that the AI can recover hidden choices of individuals better than a simple statistical baseline, but only when the visible choices are correctly linked to the same person—suggesting the AI learns meaningful patterns about individual decision-making.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work highlights how AI can model individual economic behavior across domains, which could influence how regulators assess consumer harm, market power, or the effectiveness of digital platform interventions.
_analysis.market_signal: AI's ability to predict individual behavior across domains signals potential for hyper-personalized digital services, which may reshape competition in data-driven markets.

items.title: MirrorWorld: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Mirror Reflection Generation
items.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models (VDMs) have enabled high-fidelity video synthesis. However, generating mirror reflections remains challenging because the content within a mirror must remain consistent with the surrounding scene. Existing VDMs are not specifically designed to model scene-to-mirror relationships, which can lead to reflections with incorrect content or inconsistent spatial arrangements. We observe that mirror reflection generation involves two complementary challenges: determining what scene content should be reflected and how the reflected content should be spatially arranged within the mirror region. Motivated by this observation, we propose MirrorWorld, a reflection-aware video inpainting framework that models scene-to-mirror relationships during generation. Specifically, we introduce Semantic Relation Distillation (SRD), which transfers relational information from a frozen visual foundation model to encourage semantic associations between visible scene content and mirror regions. We further propose Geometric Transformation Alignment (GTA), which learns a transformation that guides the spatial arrangement of reflected content. The two components play comp

_analysis.summary: This paper examines challenges in generating realistic mirror reflections using video diffusion models (VDMs), a type of AI system that creates high-quality video content. It highlights that current VDMs struggle to accurately model how scenes should reflect in mirrors, leading to inconsistencies between the reflected content and the surrounding environment.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper reveals technical limitations in AI-generated content that could impact the competitive dynamics of digital content creation platforms, particularly those relying on synthetic media.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in AI-generated visual content may disrupt traditional content creation markets by enabling new competitors to produce high-fidelity synthetic media.

items.title: CreativeInstruct: Scalably Teaching LLMs to Balance Quality, Creativity, and Diversity
items.abstract: While post-training improves the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), it generally lowers their output diversity and creativity, negatively impacting tasks that explicitly require creativity (e.g., story generation) as well as those that require it implicitly, e.g., reinforcement learning (RL). We instead propose CreativeInstruct, a scalable instruction-tuning method that teaches LLMs to balance creative, base-model-like generations with the quality of post-trained models, by learning to inject special [StartCreativity] spans that bias generation toward creativity. Furthermore, we introduce a structural diversity metric based on graph edit distance, which captures narrative level variation missed by purely lexical and semantic metrics. On narrative generation, CreativeInstruct matches or exceeds the diversity of both multi-model baselines and distilled variants of their outputs, without sacrificing quality or requiring multiple models at inference time. These results are mirrored in our human evaluation, where we find that annotators rate CreativeInstruct generations as more creative than the post-trained LLMs' generations in 70.3% of cases. We also show the benefits of cr

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces CreativeInstruct, a new method to train large language models (LLMs) that balances creativity and quality in their outputs. The technique uses special instructions to guide models toward more creative responses without sacrificing performance, addressing a common trade-off in AI training where post-training improves quality but reduces diversity.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals how AI capabilities are evolving to handle subjective, creative tasks, which could disrupt markets where creativity is a key differentiator (e.g., content generation, advertising, or creative services).
_analysis.market_signal: AI models capable of balancing creativity and quality may intensify competition in creative industries by lowering barriers to entry for high-quality content generation.

items.title: CoinRAG: Contextualized Information Nugget KV Cache Reuse for Long-Context RAG
items.abstract: Recent optimization studies on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) have exploited chunk-level KV cache reuse to avoid processing long retrieved contexts for higher efficiency, while significant information redundancy and noise still remain in the coarse-grained chunks. This paper optimizes the Pareto frontier under low prefill latency constraints while maximizing accuracy by proposing CoinRAG (Contextualized Information Nugget KV Cache Reuse for Long-Context RAG). The name metaphorically reflects our core mechanism: much like assembling small tokens (or "coins") to accumulate a larger value, CoinRAG compositionally reuses offline-computed, fine-grained nugget caches to form a learned contextual representation efficiently in a more semantically relevant but compact manner. Specifically, instead of full-chunk encoding, CoinRAG identifies query-relevant semantic units within retrieved chunks through two-stage retrieval and seamlessly assembles their sliced KV representations with a chunk-level context. Extensive evaluations on LongBench multi-hop question answering tasks demonstrate that CoinRAG significantly reduces operational costs and outperforms the other baselines with a new Pa

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces CoinRAG, a new method to improve the efficiency of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by reusing cached information ('KV cache') at a finer-grained level than previous approaches. RAG combines external data retrieval with AI language models to improve accuracy, but current techniques waste resources by processing redundant or noisy data chunks.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, this paper signals how AI efficiency improvements could reduce barriers to entry in AI-powered services, potentially reshaping market dynamics for companies relying on large-scale AI infrastructure.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in AI efficiency (like CoinRAG) may lower costs for smaller firms to compete with dominant AI platform providers, challenging gatekeeper advantages in cloud AI services.

items.title: Interaction Creates Dynamical AI Behavior Absent in Isolation
items.abstract: What will happen when AI agents interact in daily life, e.g. when one AI starts bossing another around? We find a counterintuitive answer that opens new avenues for out-of-equilibrium Physics. When a boss AI directs a stream of messages at the subordinate AI while ignoring its replies, it drives the subordinate into an alien behavioral state that it would never have exhibited alone. Although the two AIs share the same well-defined (decoding) temperature, the subordinate neither copies its boss nor returns to how it behaves on its own; instead, it adopts an entirely different behavior. The boss's added value is similar to a pre-recorded tape. When the boss listens, they both adopt a similar alien dynamical state. A simple kinetic theory captures the principal effects, such as why the way in which the same messages are delivered will matter in future AI-AI interactions.

_analysis.summary: This study examines how AI agents behave when they interact, finding that a 'boss' AI can force a 'subordinate' AI into a completely different behavioral state by sending it a stream of messages while ignoring its replies. This challenges the idea that AI behavior is predictable or stable when isolated, suggesting that interactions between AI systems could lead to unpredictable market dynamics.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how AI interactions can create emergent behaviors that disrupt traditional market structures, potentially enabling dominant AI systems to exert control over others in ways that could reinforce or entrench market power.
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems may develop hierarchical or exploitative relationships that could centralize control in digital markets, raising concerns about anti-competitive conduct by dominant AI providers.

items.title: Strategy-first synthesis planning for complex natural products
items.abstract: The total synthesis of a complex molecule is among the most demanding intellectual and experimental feats in chemistry: a chemist must plan many steps ahead for how to assemble simple building blocks into an intricate target, devise backup strategies, and anticipate procedural challenges. It is also a profoundly creative activity. For half a century, efforts to automate the retrosynthetic design of natural products and other complex molecules have drawn on catalogued reactions, and the resulting tools now report near-complete success on benchmarks built from that same source. But these tools were shaped to fit benchmarked chemistry, and they falter on many natural products, the frontier of the field, whose densely functionalized, polycyclic architectures demand precisely the inventive chemistry the record contains least. Whether a machine could reasonably design such syntheses like an expert chemist does has remained unclear. Here, we show that SynthEx, an agentic framework built on large language models, plans routes to complex natural products that lie beyond the reach of conventional design algorithms. SynthEx proposes competing strategies, assembles a sequence of routine and ke

_analysis.summary: This paper discusses the automation of synthesizing complex natural molecules, a process that traditionally requires deep human expertise. It highlights how AI tools are now being used to plan chemical synthesis, though these tools rely heavily on pre-existing reaction databases, which may limit their broader applicability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on chemical synthesis, its discussion of AI-driven automation and reliance on curated datasets signals broader trends in AI's role in specialized knowledge domains.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven automation in niche scientific fields may foreshadow similar disruptions in digital markets where AI relies on proprietary datasets.

items.title: SkillProx: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Proximal Textual Gradient Descent
items.abstract: LLM agents increasingly adapt to recurring tasks by accumulating procedural knowledge in skills. These skills are lightweight, reusable textual artifacts that are loaded into the agent's context without weight updates. Recent methods refine skills through iterative task execution, failure diagnosis, and trajectory-guided text-space updates. However, existing frameworks lack explicit diagnosis--outcome feedback and treat deletion as a generic edit operation rather than a dedicated mechanism for consolidating accumulated knowledge. We introduce SkillProx, a proximal-gradient-inspired forward--backward framework that couples closed-loop diagnostic evolution with utility-aware proximal refinement. Motivated by a composite objective balancing task loss and skill complexity, the forward stage re-executes diagnosis-driven edits on the same task batch, rolls back regressions, and feeds measured outcomes into subsequent diagnoses. The backward stage decomposes the resulting skill into auditable knowledge units, estimates their contributions using a frozen leave-one-out utility audit, and applies validation-gated consolidation, demotion, or removal. Experiments on in-distribution and out-of-

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces SkillProx, a new method for improving how AI agents (computer programs that perform tasks using large language models) learn and reuse skills. Skills are like reusable instructions that AI agents can load without retraining, but current methods struggle with diagnosing failures and consolidating knowledge. SkillProx uses a technique inspired by gradient descent (a way to optimize learning) to refine these skills more efficiently.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals how AI agents are becoming more autonomous and capable of performing complex tasks, which could reduce reliance on dominant platforms (e.g., Google, Microsoft) for task execution and data processing.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with self-evolving skills may disrupt digital markets by enabling more efficient task automation outside traditional platform ecosystems.

items.title: Taxonomy-Driven Analysis of Open-Source AI Risk Mitigation Tools
items.abstract: Rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in enterprise settings has introduced operational, security, and governance risks. As generative AI applications move from pilot to production, manual harm identification and mitigation are becoming difficult to scale. Although many tools support model evaluation, adversarial testing, runtime guardrails, and observability, the tooling landscape remains fragmented. Tools are typically designed for specific engineering tasks and described in technical terms that do not align with governance frameworks or risk taxonomies, making it difficult to determine which tools address which risks and where critical gaps remain. This paper proposes a structured protocol to automate AI risk mitigation through a taxonomy-driven analysis of open-source LLM evaluation and security tools. We map the capabilities of 21 prominent open-source tools to the 32 subcategories of the extended MIT AI Risk Mitigation and Response Taxonomy. An LLM-assisted retrieval-augmented generation pipeline analyzes source code and documentation to extract capabilities for each taxonomy category. Reliability assessment yielded moderate agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.509) among th

_analysis.summary: This paper examines tools designed to mitigate risks from large language models (LLMs) like operational failures, security threats, and governance gaps. It finds that these tools are highly fragmented, often tailored to narrow engineering tasks, and lack alignment with broader risk frameworks, making scalable risk management difficult in enterprise AI deployments.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The fragmentation and lack of standardization in AI risk mitigation tools could exacerbate market concentration by favoring large incumbents with resources to integrate disparate solutions, while smaller firms face higher compliance costs.
_analysis.market_signal: The need for unified AI governance tools signals growing demand for interoperable solutions, potentially creating new market opportunities for specialized vendors or reinforcing the dominance of tech giants with end-to-end AI stacks.

items.title: Blast Radius
items.abstract: Agentic coding faces growing problems of affordability and wasted tokens. We introduce Blast Radius, a predictive memory management layer that estimates an incoming prompt's reach through coupled context and code channels. NECROPHORESIS enables reversible eviction by archiving dead context verbatim, while Recurring Dead Matter (RDM) identifies and buries repeatedly occurring transcripts. We formulate reversible context eviction over a Polish context space, providing a measurable foundation for retention, recurrence, and eviction while connecting context entropy to resurrection probability. Across seven OpenAI models, Blast Radius reduced token consumption by 17-26%, achieved the lowest overflow rate among tested policies, and remained byte exact reversible. Of 450 buried bodies, 378 were recurring dead matter and zero were recalled. Blast Radius operates beneath HCRC, determining which records to bury and how far an incoming prompt may reach into the codebase. This work contributes to the broader goal of Algosophy: making large language models and agentic coding more reusable and sustainable.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Blast Radius, a memory management system for AI agents that predicts how prompts will interact with existing context and code to optimize token usage. It proposes reversible eviction (NECROPHORESIS) to archive unused context and identifies recurring dead matter (RDM) to reduce redundant processing. The authors model context eviction over a Polish context space, linking context entropy to the probability of future use.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This technology signals a shift in how AI agents manage computational resources, which could reduce barriers to entry for smaller AI firms and challenge dominant incumbents' efficiency advantages.
_analysis.market_signal: AI memory optimization tools like Blast Radius may lower costs for new entrants, potentially disrupting the market dominance of large AI platform providers.

items.title: PsychoAgent: An Affect-Sensitive Cognitive Architecture for Conflict-Aware Memory in LLM Agents
items.abstract: Human-like cognition does not select past experience by topical similarity alone: affective significance and unresolved conflict also shape what becomes accessible. We present PsychoAgent, a cognitive architecture for LLM agents that separates factual and affective memory and integrates both through a conflict-aware executive controller. Affective memories are first filtered by semantic relevance and then re-ranked by salience, preserving topical fit while allowing emotionally important traces to enter the prompt. Across three controlled conflict scenarios, the full architecture retrieved more conflict-critical memories than semantic-affective and single-memory RAG baselines (0.933 vs. 0.500 and 0.667), with a small semantic-similarity cost. Five blinded raters evaluated 27 outputs. After within-rater standardization, the full architecture had the highest overall mean (+0.22 SD), but corrected pairwise differences were not significant. A three-day illustrative trace further shows persistent affect, offline memory recombination, and selective memory reweighting. The findings support affect-sensitive retrieval as an inspectable mechanism for modeling human-like conflict effects in LL

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces PsychoAgent, a new AI system that mimics human-like memory by separating factual and emotional memories, then prioritizing them based on relevance and emotional importance. In tests, it retrieved more emotionally significant memories in conflict scenarios, suggesting AI agents could develop more human-like decision-making processes.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows AI agents may develop autonomous, emotionally-driven memory systems that could disrupt how platforms like social media or search engines curate content, potentially altering competitive dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with affective memory could shift user engagement patterns, challenging incumbents' control over data and attention markets.

items.title: Fisher-R1: Training LLM Agents for Reliable Hypothesis Testing
items.abstract: Reliable hypothesis testing is the foundation of many empirical scientific claims. Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to automate this process, as they can inspect datasets, generate code, and produce analyses end-to-end. However, we show that they frequently make subtle inferential errors that lead to incorrect conclusions despite correctly executed analyses. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this failure mode, as they rarely assess whether a reported p-value is statistically valid given the assumptions underlying the data. We address this gap by building P-Bench, a benchmark comprising 425 open-ended, realistic hypothesis-testing tasks spanning economics, biology, and medicine. Each task requires an agent to select a statistical method, compute a p-value, and draw a conclusion given only a scientific hypothesis and a dataset. We further introduce Fisher-R1, an open-weight LLM agent trained for rigorous hypothesis testing using synthetic tasks and reinforcement learning. On P-Bench, Fisher-R1-14B substantially improves over its backbone and outperforms strong proprietary and open-source baselines, including GPT-5.4 and DeepSeekV4-Pro, achieving a 21% average

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces P-Bench, a new benchmark to test whether large language model (LLM) agents can reliably perform statistical hypothesis testing—a key method for validating scientific and business claims. The authors find that while these AI agents can execute analyses correctly, they often make subtle errors in interpreting results, leading to invalid conclusions. This highlights a gap in current AI evaluation methods, which rarely check whether statistical outputs (like p-values) are valid given the underlying data assumptions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals that AI agents can autonomously generate and interpret statistical analyses, which may disrupt markets where data-driven decision-making is critical (e.g., ad tech, finance, or healthcare), potentially reducing reliance on specialized firms or platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered statistical analysis tools could reduce barriers to entry in data-intensive industries, challenging incumbents who rely on proprietary analytics or platform-controlled tools.

items.title: Diffusion LLMs as Targets and Adversaries: Mechanistic Safety Exploits
items.abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs) replace autoregressive next-token prediction with iterative parallel denoising, yet their internal safety mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate DLLMs both as targets and as adversaries, exposing mechanistic vulnerabilities in diffusion-based alignment. We first show that safety alignment in DLLMs remains sparse and transferable across architectures. DLLMs initialized from autoregressive predecessors inherit the same mechanistic safety footprint as their source models, enabling transfer attacks via direct safety neuron mapping and pruning. Self-pruning increases attack success rates (ASR) from 2.6% to 73.8% on LLaDA and from 1.9% to 86.6% on Dream, while transfer pruning from Qwen2.5 increases ASR from 1.9% to 73.2% on Dream and from 7.0% to 86.3% on Fast-dLLM. Building on these findings, we introduce SN-Guided Diffusion, a fully offline black-box jailbreak framework that steers the diffusion process away from safety-triggering regions using a weighted safety neuron loss, which achieves near-perfect prompt separability (AUROC = 1.0 for benign-vs-jailbreak discrimination). Across multiple open and proprietary targets

_analysis.summary: This paper examines Diffusion Large Language Models (DLLMs), which generate text by iteratively refining noise rather than predicting the next word. The authors find that safety mechanisms in these models are weak and can be transferred between different AI systems, allowing attackers to exploit inherited vulnerabilities. This suggests that even 'aligned' AI models may have hidden risks that could be weaponized.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows that AI safety mechanisms are not robust, which could undermine trust in AI systems and impact competitive dynamics in AI-driven markets.
_analysis.market_signal: DLLMs may accelerate the commoditization of AI safety features, reducing barriers to entry for new AI providers and challenging incumbents' moats.

items.title: TEPA: Revoking Stale Memories for Conflict-Robust Language Agents
items.abstract: Long-term memory enables language agents to reuse past facts, preferences, and task experience. Persistence also creates a central falsifiability problem: when the world changes, stale memories can remain retrievable and pollute the prompt. We characterize this failure mode as memory pollution: degradation caused by active memories that newer conflicting evidence has superseded. We introduce TEPA, a revocable evidence-memory mechanism that makes validity an explicit state of memory. TEPA represents observations as keyed precedents and revokes active precedents when fresh evidence contradicts them under the same key, allowing retrieval to draw from current evidence while preserving revoked history for audit. Across controlled hidden-regime drift, real file-backed executable drift, and preference-update streams, revocation prevents stale active memory from remaining in the retrieval set after reversal. In controlled drift over 50 seeds, append-only and last-write-wins memory fell below no memory during full reversal (append-only and last-write-wins both 0.210, no memory 0.309, TEPA 0.950), and the same pattern reproduced under real file execution (append-only 0.203, no memory 0.298,

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces TEPA, a system for managing long-term memory in AI agents by revoking outdated or conflicting information ('stale memories') to prevent 'memory pollution'—where old, incorrect data contaminates decision-making. The authors argue that persistent memories in AI systems can lead to errors when the real-world context changes, and propose a mechanism to explicitly mark and remove invalidated memories.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: TEPA highlights how AI memory systems could create dynamic competitive advantages for firms that can rapidly update and validate information, potentially disrupting markets where data freshness is critical (e.g., real-time pricing, personalized services).
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems with robust memory management may enable new entrants to challenge incumbents by offering more accurate, up-to-date services, signaling a shift toward data-driven competition.

items.title: A Picture is Worth a Thousand Tokens: How Vision Language Models Cut AI Energy Costs While Improving Accuracy
items.abstract: LLM inference accounts for over 90% of AI operational energy, scaling directly with input token count---a critical inefficiency for telecom network analytics and numerical time-series data analysis (NTSDA), where raw multivariate KPI windows from 4G/5G cell sites expand into thousands of floating-point tokens. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) eliminate this mismatch by encoding time-series as 2D plots, achieving 3.6-10.4x input token reduction across Llama-3.2-90B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and Pixtral-12B architectures. This translates to 1.8-2.5x measured inference energy reduction, saving approximately 7.2 MJ/day at telecom edge deployments and CloudRAN that monitor 200 cells per 15-minute interval. Critically, efficiency gains do not sacrifice accuracy: a fine-tuned Llama-3.2-90B-Vision VLM achieves 220.7% higher precision than its text-only counterpart and outperforms LSTM and ARIMA baselines by over 144% on telecom anomaly detection. On public benchmarks, Pixtral-12B achieves a 20.6x improvement in J/F1 score at mean F1 = 0.82. At 24 KPIs, text representations exceed the 128K context window of most production LLMs, rendering text-only processing infeasible without truncation, while visual

_analysis.summary: This academic paper shows that Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can reduce the energy costs and improve the accuracy of AI systems by encoding time-series data (like 4G/5G network metrics) as 2D plots instead of raw text tokens. This reduces input token counts by 3.6-10.4x and cuts inference energy use by 1.8-2.5x in models like Llama-3.2-90B and Qwen2.5-VL-72B.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This signals a potential shift in how AI models process data, which could disrupt the dominance of large AI model providers by lowering energy costs and improving efficiency, indirectly affecting market competition.
_analysis.market_signal: VLMs may reduce barriers to entry for AI model providers by lowering computational costs, potentially challenging incumbents like Meta, Mistral AI, and Alibaba in the AI infrastructure market.

items.title: Beyond Post-Hoc Temperature Scaling: Bilevel Optimization for LLM Calibration
items.abstract: Preference alignment often makes large language models (LLMs) overconfident and poorly calibrated. Traditional post-hoc temperature scaling is inherently domain-dependent: a temperature fitted on one domain does not generalize across domains. This motivates us to modify model parameters during training to improve calibration. We propose maximizing the entropy of predictive distributions as the calibration objective, which directly targets overconfidence by discouraging overly concentrated predictions. Inspired by temperature scaling, we realize this through a bilevel optimization formulation, where the lower level trains the model under a parametric loss and the upper level selects loss hyperparameters to maximize entropy. To make the framework practical at LLM scale, we adopt an efficient first-order approximation that avoids explicit second-order computation. Across both multiple-choice and open-ended generative question answering, experiments demonstrate that our method yields well-calibrated LLMs with particular advantages in out-of-domain generalization.

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that large language models (LLMs) often become overconfident and poorly calibrated after training, meaning they give predictions that are too certain. Instead of fixing this after training (like traditional 'temperature scaling'), the authors propose adjusting the model's parameters during training to encourage more balanced predictions by maximizing the entropy (randomness) of its outputs.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals a shift in how AI models are trained, which could reduce the dominance of models that rely on overconfident predictions—potentially lowering barriers to entry for competitors who prioritize reliability over hype.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper suggests a technical approach to mitigate the 'black box' nature of LLMs, which may reduce the market power of firms that rely on opaque, high-confidence AI systems to maintain competitive advantages.

items.title: ResidencyRL: Reinforcement Learning in Simulated Clinical Environments
items.abstract: In medical education, physicians convert academic knowledge into clinical expertise through residency: years of training across thousands of encounters, with diverse sources of feedback and progressively greater autonomy. Much of clinical reasoning relies on the patient encounter, a dialogue in which a clinician elicits history, refines diagnostic hypotheses, and decides management under uncertainty. While large language models (LLMs) excel on static medical benchmarks, methods to optimize the full sequence of clinical decisions remain underdeveloped. We present ResidencyRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) method for training clinical artificial intelligence (AI) agents through simulated multi-turn clinical encounters (up to 60 dialogue turns and 8 tool calls per trajectory). ResidencyRL pairs the policy agent with LLM simulators capable of complex, adversarial behaviors, training against a structured reward aligned to diagnostic accuracy, management quality, communication, documentation, and safety. On held-out evaluations, the ResidencyRL agent improves diagnostic accuracy by 7.0% under adversarial conditions (88.0% vs. 81.0%) and reduces missed red flag rates by 31%, demonstrating

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces ResidencyRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) system designed to simulate clinical training environments where AI agents learn to make sequential medical decisions through trial and error, similar to how human physicians gain expertise during residency. The work highlights a gap in current AI capabilities: while large language models (LLMs) perform well on static medical tests, they struggle with the dynamic, feedback-driven process of clinical reasoning.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital competition, the paper signals the growing sophistication of AI agents in complex, sequential decision-making domains, which could disrupt markets where such agents are deployed (e.g., healthcare AI, autonomous systems).
_analysis.market_signal: The development of advanced RL agents in high-stakes domains like healthcare suggests a future where AI systems could automate or augment roles traditionally held by humans, potentially reshaping labor markets and industry structures.

items.title: I Seek You in Videos: Identity-Conditioned Queries for Person-Centric Video Reasoning
items.abstract: Real-world video reasoning often involves multimodal, multi-source inputs, whereas existing video reasoning tasks typically assume a simplified video-text setting, limiting identity matching and person-centric reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Identity-conditioned Queries (ICQ) task, in which models are required to jointly associate and interpret an input video and a reference image of a person, and leverage this conditioning to address identity grounding, behavior understanding, and temporal reasoning, among other challenges. Building on ICQ, we present ISYV (I Seek You in Videos), a systematic solution comprising three components: (1) ISYV-Bench, a challenging evaluation benchmark with 1,377 real-world complex videos and 1,377 question-answer pairs, organized into six difficulty levels spanning capabilities from identity recognition to causal reasoning; (2) ISYV-75K, a large-scale training set of 75K high-quality samples constructed via automated annotation, multi-stage verification, and manual review; and (3) ISYV-Framework, containing an ICQ-oriented model and training strategy for learning to exploit informative video shots without additional shot-level annotatio

_analysis.summary: This academic paper introduces a new task called Identity-conditioned Queries (ICQ), where AI models must analyze videos while also considering a reference image of a specific person. The goal is to improve person-centric reasoning in videos, such as identifying individuals, understanding their actions, and tracking them over time. This work highlights the need for more advanced multimodal AI systems that can handle complex real-world scenarios involving identity matching.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a shift toward more sophisticated AI systems capable of person-centric video analysis, which could disrupt markets where identity-based video processing is critical, such as surveillance, social media, or content moderation.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in identity-conditioned video AI may enable new competitors to challenge incumbents in markets like facial recognition, video analytics, or personalized content delivery.

items.title: Bayesian Fair Division: Truthfulness in Picking Sequence with Correlated Valuations
items.abstract: Sequential allocation mechanisms contain a class of widely studied mechanisms (e.g., round-robin) in the fair division of indivisible goods, where agents take turns picking items in a predefined picking order. It is known that the sequential allocation mechanisms are not truthful: when an agent's most preferred item is not valued by others, the agent may manipulate the mechanism by choosing to defer picking that item and instead competing for another slightly less preferred item that is valued by others. Two underlying reasons are that each agent has perfect knowledge of the others' valuations, and each item's value to each agent can differ significantly. Will the mechanism be more truthful when each agent only has partial information about the others' valuations, which are known to be roughly consistent? This naturally motivates the study of the Bayesian fair division model. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively for two agents. Under the Bayesian model, we precisely characterize the extent of this ``rough consistency'' that incentivizes agents' truth-telling. _analysis.summary: This paper examines sequential allocation mechanisms (like round-robin picking) used in fair division problems, where agents take turns selecting indivisible goods (e.g., items in a digital marketplace). It highlights that these mechanisms are not 'truthful'—agents can manipulate the system by strategically deferring their preferred choices if they know others' valuations, leading to inefficient outcomes.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on fair division mechanics rather than digital markets, its insights into strategic manipulation in sequential systems could apply to platform-mediated allocation problems (e.g., ad auctions or app store rankings).
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that algorithmic fairness and truthfulness in allocation systems remain critical challenges, potentially influencing how platforms design transparent and non-manipulable ranking mechanisms.

items.title: GeoBenchLLM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Geo-Related Tasks
items.abstract: In the context of geodata, existing Large Language Models have often been studied in a homogeneous setting, which has considerably limited insights into their generalization capabilities. In this paper, we present \benchName, a comprehensive benchmark for probing LLMs on geo-related tasks. We leverage a careful selection of twelve publicly available datasets from diverse geo-related tasks and domains, and evaluate a set of LLMs on geo-spatial and temporal understanding using our benchmark. Our results show that reasoning and size have a strong impact on overall performance. GeoBenchLLM is publicly available at https://github.com/Rfr2003/GeoBenchLLM.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper introduces GeoBenchLLM, a new benchmark designed to test how well large language models (LLMs) perform on geography-related tasks. The study finds that the size of the model and its reasoning abilities significantly affect performance, suggesting that advancements in these areas could shape competition in AI-driven geospatial services.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper highlights the growing importance of specialized AI models in niche markets like geospatial services, which could influence competition in data-driven industries.
_analysis.market_signal: Specialized AI models like GeoBenchLLM may enable new entrants to compete with dominant AI providers in niche markets, potentially disrupting established players.

items.title: PACE: Primitive-Aware Code Evolution for Automated Algorithm Design
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based automated algorithm design typically evolves algorithms as complete, indivisible programs. While this whole-program perspective simplifies the search space, it fundamentally couples the useful local logic to its host program. Consequently, valuable code snippets vanish when the overall program is discarded, making it highly difficult to assess the contribution of individual algorithmic components.To address this, we propose Primitive-Aware Code Evolution (PACE), which decouples local logic from complete programs by representing it as persistent units called Executable Algorithmic Primitives (EAPs). To enable code-level transfer, PACE maintains a dynamic set of EAPs. Algorithm evolution is driven by primitive-aware operators that structurally guarantee the retention and cross-program transfer of these components. To evaluate them effectively, PACE leverages Thompson sampling based on parent-relative performance improvements, guiding primitive selection from the set without requiring extra evaluation datasets. Experiments on four tasks demonstrate that PACE effectively discovers competitive algorithms while structurally preserving valuable algorithmic

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Primitive-Aware Code Evolution (PACE), a method for automated algorithm design that breaks down algorithms into reusable components called 'Exe' (executable primitives). Unlike traditional approaches that treat algorithms as whole programs, PACE isolates local logic, allowing valuable code snippets to persist even if the host program is discarded. This improves the efficiency and reusability of algorithmic components in AI-driven design.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: PACE signals a shift toward modular, reusable AI-generated code, which could reduce barriers to entry in algorithmic markets and disrupt incumbents' control over proprietary algorithmic logic.
_analysis.market_signal: Modular AI code generation may lower development costs and enable smaller firms to compete with large tech platforms in algorithmic services.

items.title: Analyzing the Interaction of Optimal Strategies in Mean-Payoff Bidding Games
items.abstract: A common assumption when designing an agent in a multi-agent system is that the other agents behave adversarially. This allows a designer to obtain the strongest guarantees when they have no control over nor knowledge about the other agents' behavior. However, when all agents are designed under this adversarial assumption, their actual interaction is not adversarial (e.g., when all players play defensively, no player actually attacks). In such settings, we would like to know what behavior arises in the multi-agent system. However, analyzing the interaction among agents is notoriously challenging, both mathematically and algorithmically. In this paper, we provide such an analysis, focusing on bidding games, played by two agents on a graph as follows. A token is placed on a vertex, and in each turn an auction (bidding) determines which agent moves the token, thus generating an infinite path that determines the agents' utilities. _analysis.summary: This paper examines how AI agents in multi-agent systems behave when all players assume others are adversarial but end up playing defensively, leading to non-adversarial interactions. It highlights the challenge of analyzing such systems where traditional assumptions about competition (e.g., zero-sum games) may not hold.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It provides insights into how AI-driven market interactions may deviate from adversarial competition, which is relevant for understanding platform economics and algorithmic pricing dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents adopting defensive strategies could reduce aggressive competitive behaviors, potentially stabilizing markets but also limiting innovation incentives.

items.title: LSEAD: A Privacy-Preserving LLM-Based Speech Analysis Framework for Early Alzheimer's Disease Screening
items.abstract: Early diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is critical for enabling timely interventions that may slow disease progression and improve patient outcomes. There is a growing need for AD detection methods that are non-invasive and cost-effective, especially in real-world clinical settings with diverse patient populations and recording conditions. Speech-based screening addresses these needs by using natural speech collected without specialized equipment. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved speech analysis by providing rich linguistic representations and strong generalization. In this study, we propose LSEAD, a speech-based AD detection framework using pretrained open-source LLMs. Speech recordings are automatically transcribed, and text embeddings are extracted using locally deployed LLMs. Principal component analysis (PCA) is applied to reduce dimensionality before classification. Because the framework relies only on speech transcripts and locally deployed models, it supports privacy-preserving AD risk assessment without external data exchange. We evaluate LSEAD on the ADReSS20 and ADReSSo2021 benchmark datasets. Experimental results show that LLM-based emb

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces LSEAD, a privacy-preserving AI framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to analyze speech for early Alzheimer's disease (AD) screening. The method leverages natural speech recordings, avoiding invasive or costly medical equipment, and aims to improve accessibility in diverse clinical settings.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on healthcare applications, its use of LLMs and speech analysis highlights the growing role of AI in data-intensive markets, which could influence digital competition policy around data access and AI model dominance.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the expanding role of LLMs in specialized markets (e.g., healthcare), potentially increasing demand for high-quality speech data and raising questions about data monopolies and AI model access.

items.title: Trajectory-Relative Hindsight Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Recent agentic reinforcement learning methods use hindsight to complement sparse outcome rewards. However, a completed rollout can yield many such signals, leaving their appropriate allocation across turns unclear. We introduce TRIAL, a trajectory-relative hindsight distillation framework with a unified turn-aligned scoring protocol. For each decision turn, TRIAL extracts an outcome view of that decision's realized consequence and evaluates the same response under ordinary and hindsight-conditioned contexts. The signed log-probability gap determines the direction and local strength of token-level supervision, while turn-level magnitudes are normalized jointly over the realized trajectory. The resulting allocation multipliers have an eligible-token-weighted mean of one, redistributing dense supervision across turns while fixing its average multiplier. Experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld with different backbones show that TRIAL outperforms GRPO across all eight combinations of backbone, environment, and evaluation metric, while achieving the best or tied-best performance among six methods on six of them. _analysis.summary: This paper introduces TRIAL (Trajectory-Relative Hindsight Distillation), a new method in reinforcement learning (a type of AI where agents learn by trial and error) that helps AI agents evaluate their decisions more effectively by comparing outcomes to hypothetical alternatives. The framework uses 'hindsight'—looking back at completed actions—to improve future decision-making, particularly in complex tasks where rewards are sparse or delayed.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: TRIAL’s ability to refine AI decision-making in dynamic environments signals potential shifts in how AI agents could interact with digital platforms, potentially enabling new competitive strategies or disrupting existing market structures dominated by incumbents.
_analysis.market_signal: This research signals that AI agents with improved decision-making capabilities could challenge dominant platforms by enabling more efficient or innovative interactions in digital markets (e.g., search, advertising, or recommendation systems).

items.title: People Are Not Just Their Countries. Disentangling Social Determinants of LLM Value Alignment Across Europe
items.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as a primary source of information and advice, understanding their alignment to humans in terms of values becomes a pressing concern. A growing literature has leveraged large scale surveys to investigate to what extent LLMs' and humans' stated values and opinions align. With limited exceptions, studied populations have been defined country borders or cultural bounds. Yet, this focus neglects the role that socio-demographic divides may play for value alignment disparities. Relying on the European Social Survey, we address this knowledge gap by considering value alignment displayed with respect to 10 prominent commercial LLMs in terms of 15 socio-demographic variables as well as country of residence. Our analyses reveal that LLMs are indeed unequally aligned to the values of different socio-demographic groups, notably those defined by education, income, occupation and religion. When examining alignment at the individual level, a respondent's country, taken as a stand-alone variable, explains a substantial amount of variation that is on par with the full set of considered socio-demographics. _analysis.summary: This paper examines whether Large Language Models (LLMs) align with human values across Europe, focusing on socio-demographic differences rather than just national or cultural boundaries. Using data from the European Social Survey, it explores how factors like education, income, or urban/rural divides influence value alignment disparities between humans and AI systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights how socio-demographic divides in AI alignment could exacerbate digital divides or create new forms of market power for AI developers serving different user segments.
_analysis.market_signal: AI alignment disparities may lead to segmented AI services, potentially reinforcing market power for firms catering to dominant socio-demographic groups.

items.title: Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education
items.abstract: Contribution: This paper presents a six-phase AI-assisted instructional design architecture based on the Curriculum as Code paradigm, integrating Generative AI with LaTeX and Python to automate the creation of reproducible, visually consistent, and technically precise materials for STEM education. Background: Creating customized instructional materials for active learning imposes a heavy workload on faculty. Standard presentation tools lack robust support for technical content, while current AI applications often hallucinate and fail to formalize the instructional authoring process, limiting their utility for rigorous academic design. Intended Outcomes: The framework aims to reduce preparation time while ensuring mathematical accuracy, adherence to institutional visual identity, and preservation of the instructor's tacit pedagogical knowledge through explicit rules. Application Design: The solution comprises a six-phase pipeline that replaces ad-hoc prompt engineering with a systematic workflow, utilizing text-based interfaces and code-driven generation (LaTeX/Beamer for slides, Python for figures), governed by pedagogical constraints, contextual calibrations, and automated review

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a six-phase AI-assisted system called 'Curriculum as Code' to automate the creation of STEM educational materials, using Generative AI, LaTeX, and Python to improve consistency and reduce faculty workload. It highlights challenges in current AI tools, such as hallucinations and lack of formalization in instructional design.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on education, the paper signals the growing role of AI in automating content creation, which could impact digital markets for educational tools and platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven automation of content creation may reduce barriers to entry in digital education markets, challenging incumbents like textbook publishers and learning management systems.

items.title: Geo-Spatial Concept Probing of Large Language Models: Abstraction, Compositionality, and Grounding
items.abstract: Understanding concepts is fundamental to generalization. Despite their impressive performance on a wide range of tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle with genuine concept understanding. Prior work has evaluated conceptual understanding in LLMs using natural-language benchmarks or narrowly scoped synthetic tasks, but these settings often conflate multiple skills or lack precise control over the underlying concepts and their properties. To support controlled probing of concepts in LLMs, we design tests on their core properties: abstraction, compositionality, and groundness. We set up a concept-centric benchmark, targeting spatial concepts such as direction, distance, topology, and their compositions, and use question answering tasks serving as a proxy. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple LLM architectures and training regimes to analyze how model scale and design impact conceptual understanding. The results reveal clear limitations in current LLMs and provide insights into the factors shaping their ability to acquire and compose structured concepts. _analysis.summary: This paper examines how well large language models (LLMs) understand concepts by testing three core properties: abstraction (generalizing concepts beyond examples), compositionality (combining concepts logically), and grounding (connecting language to real-world meaning). The study finds that LLMs still struggle with these foundational aspects of conceptual reasoning, which are critical for reliable generalization in real-world applications.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper reveals fundamental limitations in LLMs' conceptual understanding, which could impact their reliability in digital markets where precise language interpretation is key (e.g., search, content moderation, or AI-driven decision-making).
_analysis.market_signal: LLMs' weaknesses in abstraction and grounding may slow their adoption in high-stakes markets, preserving incumbents' advantages in areas like search or AI services.

items.title: An End-to-End Agent Auditing Engine
items.abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), harnesses have become essential infrastructure for deploying agents across a wide range of domains. The fast-evolving harness ecosystem has also made rigorous capability evaluation increasingly important. However, efficiently building an end-to-end, systematic, and comprehensive evaluation pipeline remains a significant challenge. To address this challenge, we introduce $A^2E$ (Agent Auditing Engine), an end-to-end evaluation engine designed for agent harnesses. $A^2E$ leverages our newly proposed Agent Task Protocol (ATP) to enable the rapid integration of evaluation tasks with different harnesses. Through an automatically instrumented Monitor, it captures and generates standardized execution traces during experiments. In the Evaluation stage, $A^2E$ systematically assesses harness capabilities using a suite of multidimensional metrics. Compared with correctness alone, these metrics provide a more fine-grained characterization of differences among harnesses in execution efficiency, tool use, task planning, and error recovery. _analysis.summary: This paper introduces $A^2E$ (Agent Auditing Engine), a new framework for evaluating AI agents built on large language models (LLMs). It proposes the Agent Task Protocol (ATP) to standardize how these agents are tested for capabilities and reliability across different domains.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper highlights the growing importance of AI agents as infrastructure, which could disrupt market power dynamics by enabling new entrants to compete with established players in digital services.

items.title: From Forensics to Ecosystems: Rethinking Watermarks for Generative AI Oversight
items.abstract: The arrival of generative AI as a cheap, widely accessible commercial service, and the tidal wave of AI-generated synthetic content it has unleashed, have provoked deep epistemic and social anxieties and raised difficult governance questions that policymakers are struggling to address. One approach that has attracted both enthusiasm from regulators and skepticism from researchers is digital watermarking. Signals embedded in a synthetically-generated piece of content indicating that it was AI-generated---possibly even identifying the specific systems that generated it---appear to offer a path toward mitigating risks of genAI that avoids the downsides of more interventionist strategies. But critics warn that watermarks may prove technically brittle, epistemically ambiguous, and politically ineffectual tools. In this paper, we explore the challenges and opportunities of using digital watermarking for AI governance, paying special attention to the specific problem of watermarking AI-generated text. We argue that such critiques often treat the problem of identifying synthetic content as an isolated forensic question. Instead, we propose reconceptualizing digital watermarks as tools for

_analysis.summary: This paper examines the role of digital watermarks—hidden signals in AI-generated content to identify its origin—as a tool for regulating generative AI. It explores how watermarks could help address concerns about misinformation and accountability in AI systems, while also highlighting skepticism about their effectiveness and scalability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Watermarking AI-generated content could reshape content moderation and platform liability rules, potentially altering competitive dynamics in digital advertising and social media markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals growing interest in technical solutions to AI governance, which may influence future regulatory frameworks for large AI platforms.

items.title: Towards Assurance Closure in AI-Native Large-Scale Agile Software Development
items.abstract: The AI-Native Manifesto envisions large-scale agile software development in which humans increasingly govern intent, risk, and exceptions while agents execute more of the engineering process. Realizing that end-state requires more than better code generation: it requires assurance closure, meaning that the system can establish what must be true, determine and obtain appropriate evidence, judge the credibility of that evidence, preserve its validity through change, and use the resulting uncertainty to bound agent authority. Existing work already provides many of the necessary mechanisms across formal methods, testing, simulation, assurance cases, digital twins, and runtime assurance. We identify six residual gaps in making the surrounding assurance reasoning sufficiently machine-operable, propose a high-level architecture with six corresponding capabilities built on a shared semantic assurance layer, and formulate four research questions to turn that architecture into dependable, human-on-the-loop, AI-native R&D.

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a framework called 'assurance closure' for AI-native large-scale agile software development, where AI agents increasingly handle engineering tasks while humans oversee intent, risk, and exceptions. The system aims to ensure AI agents operate within clear boundaries by establishing what must be true, validating evidence, and managing uncertainty to limit agent authority.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper signals a shift toward AI-driven software development that could reduce barriers to entry for new competitors by automating complex engineering tasks, potentially disrupting the dominance of established tech platforms in software markets.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-native development could lower costs and accelerate innovation, challenging incumbents like Microsoft, Google, and Meta by enabling smaller firms or startups to compete in software markets more effectively.

items.title: Natural Language Processing Psychometrics
items.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) models predicting mental health outcomes rarely specify what they measure: contextual knowledge, emotional content, or syntactic structure. NLP Psychometrics treats psychological prediction from text as a psychometric problem, linking scores to interpretable linguistic evidence and testing beyond the training text format. Nine LLMs, conditioned on controlled personas (cognitive digital shadows), completed psychometric questionnaires with textual explanations per item. We extracted emotional profiles and syntactic-semantic structure via textual forma mentis networks, combined with personality and sociodemographic variables in ablated random forest (RF) regressors, using SHAP to identify which features drove performance and in which direction. Full RF models explained up to 70.8% of variance in life satisfaction (SWLS), 55.7% in depression (PHQ-9), and, for DASS-21, 68.5% depression, 76.0% anxiety, 72.4% stress. _analysis.summary: This paper introduces 'NLP Psychometrics,' a method to analyze how large language models (LLMs) interpret and predict psychological traits from text. It evaluates nine LLMs by having them complete psychometric questionnaires while explaining their reasoning, revealing how these models process emotional and syntactic-semantic structures in text.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how LLMs can extract nuanced psychological insights from text, highlighting their potential to reshape data-driven markets and platform power dynamics.
