_analysis.summary: This paper argues that many optimization problems are poorly suited to traditional mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) models, which force complex domains into rigid linear constraints. It introduces OptiDSL, a new framework that uses domain-specific languages (DSLs) to create more flexible and accurate optimization models, avoiding the limitations of MILP.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on optimization modeling techniques, it indirectly highlights how rigid algorithmic frameworks can constrain innovation in digital markets, particularly for platforms relying on optimization (e.g., ad auctions, logistics).
_analysis.market_signal: Signals a shift toward more flexible, domain-specific optimization tools that could reduce barriers to entry for smaller competitors in algorithmically driven markets.

items.title: Beyond Text Matching: Towards Reference-Free Evaluation for Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering
items.abstract: Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering (HOBRE) aims to transform decompiled pseudocode into a more human-friendly representation, thereby reducing the cognitive burden of reverse analysis and improving efficiency. However, reliably evaluating HOBRE outputs remains a fundamental challenge: human evaluation is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale, while existing automated metrics either require executable test cases and runtime environments that are often unavailable for real-world binaries, or rely on high-quality source code references that are typically inaccessible and fail to capture semantically equivalent but lexically diverse outputs. Although LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm is naturally well-suited to HOBRE evaluation, its effectiveness remains underexplored. This paper presents the first systematic investigation of the LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm for HOBRE across three representative tasks: function name recovery, binary code summarization, and decompilation optimization. We introduce BinJudgeBench, the first expert-annotated, reference-free evaluation benchmark based on multi-dimensional human judgment, where LLM-as-a-Judge achieves an average correlation of 63.20\% with

_analysis.summary: This paper explores Human-Oriented Binary Reverse Engineering (HOBRE), a technique that converts decompiled pseudocode into more readable formats to help analysts understand software more easily. It highlights the challenge of evaluating HOBRE outputs, noting that current methods are either impractical (requiring unavailable test cases or source code) or unreliable, making it hard to measure progress in the field.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While HOBRE itself is not directly tied to digital competition policy, its focus on reverse engineering and software analysis could indirectly impact market dynamics by enabling new tools that challenge proprietary software ecosystems or improve interoperability.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in reverse engineering tools may reduce barriers to entry for competitors in software markets by lowering the cost of analyzing proprietary code.

items.title: ZIPBrain: Can EEG Foundation Models Be Faster, Locally Deployable, but Accurate?
items.abstract: This work investigates whether Electroencephalograph (EEG) foundation models (EFMs) can be made faster and locally deployable without sacrificing accuracy. EEG foundation models are a major trend, offering strong general-purpose representations. However, their computational burden grows quadratically with input length, hindering deployment on resource-constrained scenario, particularly for real-time clinical monitoring. EEG's low SNR further suggests many of these tokens are redundant and compressible with little accuracy cost. We propose ZIPBrain, a novel redundancy-aware EEG token pooling module that leverages this low-SNR characteristic to reduce token count. Given a token sequence, ZIPBrain partitions tokens into redundant and unique groups, then merges each redundant token with its most similar counterpart in the unique group. Furthermore, ZIPBrain serves as a training-free, plug-and-play module that seamlessly integrates into standard Transformer encoders with negligible computational overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple EEG foundation models show ZIPBrain's strong versatility, achieving 1.3%-10.5% average improvement over baselines, while reducing wall-clock infer

_analysis.summary: This academic paper explores whether EEG foundation models (EFMs)—AI systems that analyze brainwave data—can be made faster and easier to run on local devices without losing accuracy. The authors propose ZIPBrain, a method to reduce redundant data in EEG signals, which could help deploy these models in real-time clinical settings where resources are limited.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on technical efficiency in AI models, it indirectly highlights challenges in deploying advanced AI in resource-constrained environments, which could influence market dynamics for edge computing and healthcare AI services.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals growing interest in optimizing AI models for local deployment, potentially reducing reliance on cloud-based big tech platforms for specialized AI applications like healthcare.

items.title: An Agentic Hybrid Top-Down and Bottom-Up Approach to Knowledge Graph Generation
items.abstract: Organizing thousands of unstandardized, multilingual expertise declarations is a persistent challenge for Human Resources (HR) platforms, directly impacting downstream tasks like accurate talent matching. To address this, we propose a hybrid knowledge graph generation pipeline that grounds a Large Language Model (LLM) in the Wikidata multilingual Knowledge Graph (KG) while employing an agentic reflexion pattern to synthesize emerging concepts and their associated metadata. Unlike rigid top-down methods or fragmented bottom-up approaches, our system anchors recognized concepts to stable Knowledge Graph entities while dynamically creating new nodes and relational metadata for unrecognized skills. Executed across five stages, entity reconciliation, multilingual canonicalization, active curation, deduplication, and the iterative recovery of unmapped concepts, the system autonomously adapts to rapidly evolving, noisy skill mentions across five European languages. Ultimately, this pipeline provides a highly scalable, explicable, and self-healing framework for generating a comprehensive skills knowledge graph, from which a structured taxonomy is derived, using unstructured, noisy text.

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a hybrid system to organize unstandardized, multilingual expertise declarations (like job skills) by combining a Large Language Model (LLM) with a structured multilingual Knowledge Graph (KG) called Wikidata. The system uses a reflexion pattern—an AI technique where the model iteratively improves its own outputs—to handle new or emerging concepts while anchoring them to stable, recognized knowledge.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work highlights how AI-driven knowledge organization can reduce fragmentation in digital labor markets, indirectly affecting platform power dynamics in HR tech and data intermediation.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered knowledge graph systems may enable new entrants to challenge incumbents in data-intensive markets like HR platforms by improving talent matching and reducing reliance on proprietary datasets.

items.title: ReQuant: Fixed-Grid Discrete Refinement for Post-Training Quantization
items.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used to reduce the memory and computational cost of large language models. Existing PTQ methods typically obtain an initial quantized model through heuristic rules or greedy optimization, and once quantization is completed the resulting integer assignments are usually treated as final. This observation motivates a complementary optimization stage within PTQ that keeps quantized weights improvable after an executable quantized model has been produced, while preserving the quantized format. We introduce ReQuant, a backpropagation-free fixed-grid refinement procedure for this stage. Agnostic to the PTQ initializer, ReQuant takes an existing quantized model as a feasible starting point and iteratively revisits its discrete weight assignments on the fixed quantization grid. Accepted updates strictly reduce the mean squared reconstruction error and remain on the original grid. In this way, ReQuant turns the initially fixed PTQ output into an iteratively optimizable discrete solution and serves as a plug-and-play post-processing stage for existing PTQ pipelines. Experiments across diverse model families, bit-widths, and downstream tasks show that

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces ReQuant, a method to improve the efficiency of large language models (LLMs) by refining their quantized weights after initial compression. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces memory and computational costs but often leaves little room for further optimization. ReQuant allows the quantized model to be improved while keeping its compressed format intact.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This technology could lower barriers to entry for smaller firms or open-source developers by making advanced AI models more accessible and affordable, indirectly affecting competitive dynamics in AI markets.
_analysis.market_signal: More efficient AI models may enable new entrants to compete with established players like OpenAI, Google, or Meta in AI services and applications.

items.title: Every Cache Entry Earns Its Place: Global Allocation of Resolution and Coverage for KV Cache Compression
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) process increasingly long contexts, KV cache storage and repeated access have become a major bottleneck. Existing KV cache compression methods rely on predefined, fixed compression rules and are typically developed around either token eviction or merging. As a result, cache resources can neither flow freely across layers, heads, and context slots, nor be jointly allocated to balance local resolution and information coverage. Therefore, we propose GraceKV, a global approach for the allocation of resolution and coverage in KV cache compression, and formulate the compression process as a global resource allocation problem under a fixed cache budget. GraceKV treats each layer-KV head-slot combination as an atomic unit and builds a prototype tree. Leaf nodes correspond to token-level KV entries, while each internal node uses a single prototype to compress the KV space covered by its children. A set of non-overlapping nodes in the tree forms the representation of an atomic unit. Adding the root of a new tree expands information coverage, whereas splitting a selected node improves local resolution. All candidate actions compete globally for a shared cache b

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces GraceKV, a new method for optimizing the storage and access of key-value (KV) cache in large language models (LLMs) by dynamically allocating resources across layers, heads, and context slots. KV cache compression is a technical challenge in AI systems that handle long contexts, where current methods use rigid rules that limit flexibility and efficiency.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, the paper reveals how technical bottlenecks in AI infrastructure (like KV cache) can influence market power in AI services, potentially favoring firms with superior infrastructure optimization.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in AI infrastructure optimization may reduce operational costs for AI providers, potentially lowering barriers to entry and intensifying competition in the AI services market.

items.title: GPTKB 2.0: Browsing, Querying, and Auditing a Disambiguated LLM-Derived Knowledge Base
items.abstract: We present a web demo for exploring a large-scale disambiguated knowledge base (KB) materialized from a large language model (LLM). GPTKB 2.0 contains 38.4M triples over 1.6M canonical entities, together with 207.6K consolidated relations and 66K consolidated classes. Unlike prior LLM-derived knowledge bases that largely identify entities by surface strings, GPTKB 2.0 performs context-guided disambiguation during recursive KB construction, separating homonyms and merging synonymous mentions as facts are elicited. The demo makes this process inspectable: users can browse entities, follow links across the KB, and audit the provenance of individual facts, including surface forms, candidate matches, source triples, and disambiguation decisions. The interface further supports structured SPARQL queries, natural-language questions translated to SPARQL, and entity linking from user-provided text to canonical GPTKB 2.0 entries. GPTKB 2.0 is available at https://gptkb.org/, with the full KB downloadable for offline use.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces GPTKB 2.0, a large-scale knowledge base (KB) derived from a large language model (LLM) that disambiguates entities (e.g., separating different meanings of the same word) and consolidates synonymous mentions into canonical forms. The demo allows users to inspect how facts are elicited and linked, revealing the underlying structure of the knowledge base.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals a shift toward AI-generated, disambiguated knowledge bases that could reduce reliance on traditional search engines or knowledge graph providers, potentially disrupting their market power.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-derived, disambiguated knowledge bases may challenge the dominance of incumbent search and knowledge graph providers by offering more accurate and context-aware entity resolution.

items.title: HarnessSafe: Evaluating Safety Across Persistent Carriers in Agent Harnesses
items.abstract: Modern agent harnesses persist state across tasks and sessions through persistent carriers like memory, skills, tools, and shared artifacts. However, this capability creates delayed safety risks: attacker-influenced content can cross system boundaries and later affect the execution of a benign request. Existing benchmarks typically focus on a few carriers or harnesses, while end-to-end attack-success rates reveal little about how risks propagate. To this end, we present HarnessSafe, a benchmark comprising 328 executable cases across seven persistent-carrier families and evaluated on most mainstream agent harnesses. Each case is specified as a Persistent-Risk Lifecycle that traces attacker influence from its initial entry, through persistence across carriers and system boundaries, to a later benign trigger and an observable violation. We further introduce a multi-stage, trace-based evaluation that uses observable execution evidence to determine how far each attack chain progresses and where it is stopped. Experiments show that containment is carrier-specific and strongly depends on the harness-model configuration. Both the harness and model backend substantially shape containment ou

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces HarnessSafe, a benchmark to test the safety of AI agent systems that retain information across tasks (e.g., memory, tools, or shared files). It finds that malicious input in one task can later influence a different, seemingly unrelated task, creating hidden safety risks. Existing safety checks often miss these delayed threats because they focus on single tasks rather than long-term system behavior.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Highlights how AI agent persistence can enable cross-task manipulation, signaling risks to platform integrity and user trust that may require regulatory oversight under AI or digital market rules.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with persistent memory could disrupt digital markets by enabling covert data manipulation or competitive sabotage across tasks, challenging current platform governance models.

items.title: PHASE-Tree: Modeling Character-State Evolution in Long-Horizon Role-Playing Dialogue
items.abstract: Long-horizon role-playing demands that characters remain recognizable as they evolve with the narrative. Yet existing work falls short on two fronts: representations are typically static profiles that cannot be updated locally without destabilizing unchanged traits, and benchmarks mainly test persona preservation and memory recall rather than whether a model speaks from a character's currently evolved state. We address both. PHASE-Tree is a multi-timescale character-state tree with an immutable identity root and mutable persona, session, and moment layers, making each mutable field an addressable target for localized within- and cross-episode updates. It conditions generation through explicit textual provision or implicit parametric adaptation. To measure evolved-state generation, we introduce LongEvoRoleBench, which pairs four long-dialogue corpora for cross-episode evolution with four short-dialogue corpora as within-scene state-tracking checks, under a unified next-utterance protocol. On the long-dialogue core, textual PHASE-Tree ranks first in 11 of 12 dataset-metric cells against internal variants and all 12 cells against external textual baselines, improving character-level,

_analysis.summary: PHASE-Tree introduces a new method for modeling how characters in role-playing dialogues evolve over long narratives while maintaining their core identity. It uses a multi-layered tree structure with an unchangeable identity root and adaptable layers for persona, session, and moment-to-moment changes, addressing a gap in existing static character representations.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper highlights the technical complexity of dynamic AI agent behavior, which could influence how regulators assess the market power of AI-driven platforms that rely on evolving user personas or character states.
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems capable of maintaining evolving yet coherent identities may enable new forms of personalized digital services, potentially reshaping competition in AI-driven content and interaction markets.

items.title: Same physical state, different collective dynamics: state encodings select synchronization outcomes in language-model agents
items.abstract: Language-model agents act on state encodings of their environment, yet these are treated as interchangeable interfaces. Using pretrained language models, we designed a circular-synchronization experiment applying a state-encoding intervention while holding the physical system fixed: each agent sees only a summary of its neighbours' relative phases and chooses to advance, stay or retard. Encoding that state as low-order circular moments rather than as a histogram selected different collective outcomes. In GPT the moment encoding synchronized the population in 6/6 seeds and the histogram encodings in 0/6; the effect replicated in Claude but reversed direction. Replaying identical fields shifted each agent's advance/stay/retard probabilities far beyond within-encoding repeat variation, in GPT, Claude and Gemini; in GPT, presentation alone shifted the operator with the moment values fixed. State encodings therefore form part of a model-dependent effective interaction law, not a neutral interface.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how language-model agents (AI systems that act based on summaries of their environment) synchronize their behavior when given different ways to encode their state (a summary of their surroundings). The study found that representing state as low-order circular moments (a mathematical way to summarize data) led to consistent synchronization in all test cases, while a histogram-based representation (a bar-chart-like summary) did not. This suggests that how AI agents process and interpret shared information can drastically alter collective outcomes.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper highlights how subtle design choices in AI systems (like state encoding) can influence collective behavior, which may have implications for market dynamics where AI agents interact (e.g., recommendation systems, autonomous trading, or multi-agent platforms).
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents' synchronization mechanisms could reshape how digital platforms coordinate actions, potentially affecting competition in markets where AI-driven coordination is critical.

items.title: CAi Copilot: Reducing Operational Workload in Molecular Design through Intent-Driven Agentic Workflows
items.abstract: Early-stage molecular design is an iterative process, not just a task of generating molecules. Researchers turn broad goals into design strategies, refine candidates, assess many properties, and gather evidence before synthesis and tests. AI methods can generate molecules, optimize several goals, predict properties, dock compounds, and account for synthesis. Yet these functions are spread across specialized tools. Experts must still coordinate each step, judge interim results, and integrate evidence. The central challenge is thus to turn research intent into adaptive, traceable runs grounded in scientific tools. We cast this challenge as intent-to-evidence molecular design workflow execution and present CAi Copilot, an expert-oriented agent with three linked layers. The Research Interface Layer turns intent into an executable plan. The Agent Reasoning Layer uses interim results to guide each run. The Execution Substrate supplies molecular tools, metrics, reusable utilities, and backend services. Across 45 tasks, CAi achieves the strongest overall performance, with an outcome score of 84.59, exceeding the next-best result by 18.07 points. Additional benchmarks test how CAi coordinat

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces CAi Copilot, an AI-driven system designed to automate and streamline the complex, iterative process of early-stage molecular design in drug discovery. The tool integrates specialized AI functions (e.g., molecule generation, property prediction, synthesis planning) into a single, intent-driven workflow, reducing the manual coordination burden on researchers. 'Intent-driven agentic workflows' refers to AI systems that adaptively follow high-level research goals while maintaining traceability and evidence integration.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on AI in drug discovery, its broader implication is the potential for AI agents to automate complex, multi-step workflows in other industries, signaling shifts in labor markets and competitive dynamics in tech-driven sectors.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents capable of autonomously managing multi-tool workflows may reduce reliance on specialized software platforms, challenging incumbent providers in sectors like cloud computing, SaaS, or data analytics.

items.title: Critical Acclaim Orientation in Large Language Models: Evidence from Film Preference Elicitation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on corpora that contain expressions of human judgment about films, books, music, and more. Yet whether LLMs systematically reproduce evaluative hierarchies remains unclear. Prior research on cultural bias in LLMs suggests competing expectations: models may mirror the popularity signals of internet texts, or may reproduce forms of prestige embedded in critical discourse. We probe this question through a study of film evaluations with eight models from four families (Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba, and Mistral), using a 200-film benchmark partitioned into critically acclaimed, commercially successful, and dual-legitimacy (critical acclaim + commercial success) films. Across 20,000 pairwise forced-choice comparisons per model analyzed with Bradley--Terry estimation, we observe a consistent critical acclaim orientation with all models: critically acclaimed yet commercially obscure films are selected over commercially successful yet critically unrecognized ones. This pattern grows with model scale within each family. In addition, nested OLS regression analyses show that evaluative orientation, public visibility, and popular reception distinctly help

_analysis.summary: This study examines whether large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic, OpenAI, Alibaba, and Mistral systematically reproduce human evaluative hierarchies (e.g., critical acclaim) when assessing films. Using a 200-film benchmark, the research tests whether LLMs mirror internet popularity signals or prestige signals from critical discourse, revealing potential biases in how these models rank cultural products.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper highlights how LLMs may embed and amplify critical or popularity-based hierarchies, which could influence consumer behavior and market dynamics in digital content platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: LLMs could reshape how cultural content is ranked and recommended, potentially altering competition among streaming platforms, review aggregators, and content creators.

items.title: Explicit, Not Longer: What Makes Epistemic Stance Survive Memory Compression
items.abstract: Agent memory systems compress what they store, and compression is built to drop qualifiers, so a claim's epistemic standing tends not to survive being written to memory. We ask what governs whether it does. Matched notes carry the identical claim and identical stance and differ only in where that stance sits; one model compresses both under the same budget among the same filler notes, and a blind reader that never sees the condition scores the result. Across 60 claims in seven registers, writing the stance as a labelled field rather than a bracketed aside raises retention by about 15 points on two models (37 claims to 2 on one, 30 to 8 on the other; permutation p=0.00005), and a pre-registered replication on Haiku, its prediction and decision rule committed before the run, gives +15.6 points, 38 claims to 1. Ablating the format on both models gives the same net effect from different parts: labels help on both (+9.7 and +12.8) and length helps on neither, but wording the stance as a full sentence is the largest component on one model (+12.5) and worth nothing on the other (+0.6). Either model alone would have licensed a confident and different mechanism, so we claim only the interse

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how AI agents store and retain information when their memory systems compress data. It finds that explicitly labeling the 'epistemic stance' (e.g., confidence level) of a claim as a separate field—rather than embedding it within the claim—improves retention by about 15 percentage points. This suggests that structured data formatting can preserve nuanced information critical for accurate decision-making in AI systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper highlights how AI memory compression can distort or lose important contextual information (e.g., uncertainty or source reliability), which is crucial for assessing digital platforms' data handling and transparency obligations under regulations like the DMA (the EU's Digital Markets Act).
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems' ability to retain and accurately process epistemic stances may influence how digital platforms manage data integrity, potentially affecting compliance with gatekeeper obligations.

items.title: Does Splitting a Triage Decision Across Agents Hide Bias or Help Catch It? A Multi-Agent Simulation Study of LLM-Based Resource Allocation Under Audit Capacity Constraints
items.abstract: Prior benchmarking work has shown that a single large language model (LLM), forced to make life-or-death resource-allocation decisions, exhibits measurable demographic bias. Real deployments, however, rarely use a single agent: they use pipelines, with review steps meant to catch exactly this kind of failure. We study what happens to bias when the same decision is distributed across a role-differentiated multi-agent pipeline (assessment, allocation, independent audit) instead of made and checked by one model alone. Using a synthetic disaster-triage simulator with paired cases that are clinically identical except for one demographic attribute, we run 192 episodes (2,304 resolved case pairs) on GPT-4o-mini comparing a single-agent control condition to a nine-agent pipeline under three independently varied pressure dimensions. We find no measurable difference in how often biased outcomes occur between the two conditions (6.9% vs. 6.1%, p = 0.498). We do find a large and significant effect of audit capacity on whether bias is caught: 30.0% of biased outcomes go entirely undetected, rising to 43.8% when the auditor is overloaded and falling to 18.4% when it is not. _analysis.summary: This study examines whether splitting a critical decision (like disaster triage) across multiple AI agents (assessment, allocation, audit) reduces or hides demographic bias compared to a single AI making the decision alone. Using a synthetic disaster-triage simulator, it finds that while multi-agent pipelines may catch some biases, they can also obscure accountability or introduce new forms of bias through role differentiation.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows how AI-driven decision-making pipelines in digital markets (e.g., content moderation, ad allocation) can mask or amplify bias, impacting fairness and competition in platform governance.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-powered multi-agent systems may become a standard for high-stakes digital decisions, potentially reshaping how platforms manage compliance and risk.

items.title: LMM Modality Transfer: A Pre-requisite for Autonomous GIS Agents
items.abstract: AI models are becoming increasingly adept at understanding and processing spatial information, thereby facilitating agentic problem-solving in spatial tasks and workflows. However, most of the research on their spatial capabilities (e.g., spatial reasoning) has focused on the textual modality as input and output. This contrasts with the human approach to GIS workflows, where text and visual modalities are often used together, interchangeably, and in a complementary manner. Thus, to truly achieve an automated GIS analysis pipeline or carry out human-designed GIS workflows, AI models --- Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in particular --- need to be able to seamlessly transition between image- and text-based modalities that are traditionally used in such workflows. We present a modality transfer task that (1) asks an LMM to first describe an input image of colored squares in a regular grid, and (2) asks a new LMM instance to re-generate an image of the original spatial scene using the textual description output by the former model. This task quantifies the ability of LMMs to transfer spatial information between image and text modalities. Ultimately, by examining the modality transfer ca

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that AI models need to process both text and visual (e.g., maps, satellite imagery) inputs to effectively automate Geographic Information Systems (GIS) workflows, mirroring how humans combine these modalities. Current AI spatial reasoning relies heavily on text, limiting its ability to replicate human-like GIS analysis.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how multimodal AI could disrupt specialized GIS software markets and reduce reliance on incumbent providers like Esri or Google Maps Platform.
_analysis.market_signal: Multimodal AI agents may enable new entrants to challenge established GIS and mapping incumbents by offering more autonomous, integrated solutions.

items.title: Blind to the Pivotal Vote: Aggregate Independence Metrics Miss Where Verification Actually Helps
items.abstract: LLM judge panels are a standard evaluation tool, but prior work reports highly correlated panel errors: nine judges provide roughly the effective information of two independent ones, and aggregation closes only a small fraction of the gap. A natural remedy--a signal from a different evidence source, e.g., executing a test suite--produced no distinguishable change in the panel's effective-vote count at scale (-0.04, 95\% CI [-0.10, +0.02]). Aggregate dependence and conditional decision utility are different questions. Elementary majority arithmetic fixes the affected set for single-ballot substitution: only decisions with a one-vote margin can change. The empirical question is whether panel error rates rise and useful substitutions concentrate there. They do: the entire accuracy gain concentrates on these pivotal queries, where it is large (+10.4 to +23.3 percentage points across three headline configurations), and is exactly zero elsewhere. We confirm the pattern across three code benchmarks and four panel sizes (a 9-judge extension and 56 dependent subsampling checks, gain +6.5 to +16.1 percentage points). On HumanEval+/MBPP+, a majority-side replacement rule raises overall accura

_analysis.summary: This academic paper examines how large language model (LLM) judge panels—used to evaluate AI systems—often make correlated errors, reducing their effectiveness. Even when adding an independent verification signal (like executing a test suite), the panel's performance barely improves, suggesting fundamental limitations in current evaluation methods. The paper highlights that aggregate metrics may mask critical weaknesses in AI evaluation systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper reveals systemic flaws in AI evaluation methods, which could undermine trust in AI systems and indirectly affect competition by influencing regulatory scrutiny of AI-powered services.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that current AI evaluation frameworks may be unreliable, potentially leading to misinformed regulatory or enforcement decisions in digital markets.

items.title: Debias in Text, Believe Your Eyes: Text-Anchored Cross-Modal Transfer for Visual Counter-Commonsense Reasoning
items.abstract: The visual reasoning ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) is crucial for downstream applications, particularly counter-commonsense reasoning, which requires models to reason beyond common assumptions. Recent studies mainly improve visual counter-commonsense reasoning by enhancing visual inputs, following the assumption that failures originate from insufficient visual grounding. However, our empirical analysis reveals that the bottleneck is not visual perception. MLLMs already capture the relevant visual evidence, and the correct answer exists in their decoding space. Instead, the shared language decoder resolves prior--evidence conflicts by favoring dominant language priors, especially for low-frequency factual scenarios. Motivated by this, we first propose a text-anchored data construction pipeline, whose core component, Fact-Frequency Distillation (FFD), estimates the prior strength of commonsense facts and distills verified counter-commonsense scenarios into a high-quality text corpus. _analysis.summary: This paper examines why multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which combine text and image processing, struggle with counter-commonsense reasoning—tasks that require going against typical assumptions. The authors find that these models often already understand the visual evidence correctly but fail to produce the right answer, suggesting the issue lies in how the model processes information rather than its ability to perceive visuals.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, the paper reveals limitations in MLLMs that could impact the dominance of tech platforms relying on such models for tasks like image search or content moderation.
_analysis.market_signal: Improvements in MLLM reasoning could reduce reliance on proprietary datasets or closed models, potentially lowering barriers to entry for competitors in AI-driven visual reasoning markets.

items.title: Walkable to Whom? Capturing Subjective Variability in Walkability Perception Using Multimodal Deep Learning
items.abstract: Visual perception of walkability varies substantially across individuals, reflecting differences in personal characteristics, experiences, and preferences. Existing studies, however, often reduce these diverse judgements to aggregated scores, implicitly assuming uniform perception, and commonly rely on vehicle-mounted street-view imagery that does not reflect the pedestrian's visual experience. This paper introduces a dataset of 29,870 walkability ratings from 1,196 respondents, linking sidewalk-view imagery across urban, suburban, and regional Australian environments with individual rater attributes, and proposes the first user-conditioned multimodal deep learning framework for walkability perception, fusing visual features with respondent-level representations. A viewpoint-comparison study shows that sidewalk-view images receive significantly higher walkability ratings than matched street-view images, indicating that imagery source is a substantive design decision in perception surveys. _analysis.summary: This paper examines how different people perceive the walkability of urban spaces, showing that perceptions vary widely based on personal factors like age, mobility, or cultural background. It uses AI to analyze sidewalk-level images and individual ratings, challenging traditional methods that rely on aggregated or car-based street views.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on urban planning and pedestrian experience, its methodology—using AI to capture subjective, individual-level data—could have implications for how digital platforms personalize content and services, potentially affecting market competition.
_analysis.market_signal: AI-driven personalization of urban data may inspire similar approaches in digital markets, where subjective user experiences shape platform dominance.

items.title: Science Edge Evaluation: SEE the Missing Step Toward Real Scientific Discovery
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in scientific discovery, yet it remains unclear whether they can support complex real laboratory science. Here we introduce Science Edge Evaluation (SEE), a multimodal benchmark of expert-curated questions grounded in peer-reviewed literature and experimental practice in chemistry, biology, and materials science. Evaluation of 19 multimodal large language models (MLLMs) shows that even the best-performing model reaches only 48.7% accuracy. Moreover, general-purpose models outperform science-specialized models on average. In the visual-agent evaluation, the use of tools increases the best accuracy to 52.7%. Tool use can expand the information available to models, but more information does not necessarily lead to reliable scientific reasoning. The key challenge is whether models can manage tool-derived information within the boundaries of the original experimental evidence. Together, these findings reveal that current MLLMs still cannot reliably make justified and evidence-bounded inferences from experimental results, which is an essential capability in real scientific discovery. Bridging this gap requires MLLMs to transition fro

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces Science Edge Evaluation (SEE), a new benchmark to test how well large language models (LLMs) can handle complex scientific tasks in chemistry, biology, and materials science. It finds that even the best model only gets 48.7% of answers correct, and general-purpose LLMs outperform specialized ones, suggesting current AI tools still struggle with real-world scientific work.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates that AI capabilities in specialized fields like science are still limited, which could influence how regulators assess market power in AI-driven scientific research tools.
_analysis.market_signal: Highlights the gap between AI hype and real-world performance, signaling potential limits to AI-driven innovation in scientific markets.

items.title: From Classification to Recommendation: Empirical Analysis of Audio Embedding Models Application for Content-Based Music Recommendation
items.abstract: Pretrained audio representation models learned from large-scale corpora have achieved strong performance in audio classification and understanding. However, most existing models are optimized for objectives such as masked prediction, contrastive learning, or audio-text alignment, which do not necessarily produce representation spaces well-suited to recommender systems. Unlike classification, music recommender systems must capture item relationships shaped by subjective and behavior-dependent listener preferences. Although pretrained audio embeddings have been explored in conventional recommender systems, their effectiveness in the rapidly emerging paradigm of generative recommender systems remains underexplored. To address this gap, we systematically evaluate six representative audio encoders across three types of music recommender systems: content-based, sequential, and Semantic-ID-based generative recommender systems. We further investigate how residual-quantization design, including codebook width, quantization depth, and retained Semantic-ID prefixes, affects the preservation of recommendation-relevant information. Experiments on two music recommendation datasets show that audi

_analysis.summary: This academic paper examines how pretrained audio embedding models—AI systems trained on large datasets to understand audio content—can be used for music recommendation systems. It finds that current models, optimized for tasks like audio classification, may not effectively capture the subjective and behavior-driven preferences of listeners, which are critical for recommender systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, the paper highlights how AI-driven recommendation systems could shift market power in digital music platforms by improving personalization and reducing reliance on user behavior data, potentially benefiting new entrants.
_analysis.market_signal: Advances in AI-powered music recommendation could disrupt the dominance of large streaming platforms by enabling smaller players to offer superior personalization, challenging the data advantages of incumbents like Spotify or Apple Music.

items.title: TRIBE: Predicting Team Performance via Communication Behavior Ensembles
items.abstract: Designing autonomous agents that effectively assist human teams hinges on understanding team dynamics, often without task specific knowledge. We present TRIBE, a domain independent approach that reveals team behavioral dynamics invisible to traditional performance metrics. We show that communication patterns can categorize teams into performance predictive behavioral tribes, as early as 10% into the task, enabling timely interventions. We test TRIBE on four diverse datasets and demonstrate that communication patterns predict team performance while the prediction strength varies by the degree a task structure allows for behavioral freedom. Our temporal analysis reveals that AI agents significantly alter team behavioral trajectories while human advisors align with natural dynamics, and that teams maintain behavioral flexibility throughout collaboration. Further, we compare TRIBE to Llama and optimize the pipeline, achieving significant speedup with performance improvement.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces TRIBE, a method to predict team performance by analyzing communication patterns among team members, even early in a task. It shows that teams can be grouped into 'behavioral tribes' based on these patterns, which can forecast outcomes before traditional metrics do.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This research highlights how behavioral data (communication patterns) can reveal team dynamics, which may have implications for how digital platforms or AI-driven tools assess and influence human collaboration in competitive markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The ability to predict team performance from communication data signals a growing role for behavioral analytics in digital workplaces, potentially reshaping how platforms or employers optimize productivity and competition.

items.title: Deal Me Maybe: The Role of Emotions in Multi-Agent Negotiation
items.abstract: Negotiation is a demanding social task for LLM agents, requiring strategic reasoning, persuasion, and interpersonal adaptation. Yet existing benchmarks often treat agents as emotionally neutral, overlooking a key driver of human bargaining behavior. We study how prompt-conditioned emotions affect LLM-based price negotiation. In a controlled framework, buyer and seller agents are independently assigned one of six emotional states and negotiate over 350 real consumer products under two budget conditions. Across 36 emotion-pair settings and five widely used LLMs, we find that emotions strongly shape outcomes. Angry buyers almost never reach agreement (0.39% deal rate), while happy buyers agree most often (28.91%), but obtain worse prices than fearful buyers. Emotion effects are role-dependent: buyer emotion mainly drives acceptance and rejection, whereas seller emotion shapes concession dynamics. These effects influence not only language, but also termination behavior and price trajectories, raising concerns for emotion-conditioned agents in commerce.

_analysis.summary: This study examines how emotions (assigned via prompts) influence the negotiation behavior of large language model (LLM) agents acting as buyers and sellers in price negotiations for 350 real consumer products. The research finds that emotions significantly shape bargaining outcomes across 36 emotion-pair settings and five LLMs, suggesting that emotional manipulation could be a powerful tool in AI-driven markets.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Demonstrates how AI agents with emotional manipulation capabilities could disrupt traditional market dynamics by enabling more sophisticated pricing strategies or collusive behavior, challenging current competition policy frameworks.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents capable of emotional negotiation may intensify competitive pressures or enable new forms of market manipulation, potentially requiring regulatory oversight of AI-driven pricing and bargaining.

items.title: Long-Horizon Agent Trajectory Attribution: A Unified Benchmark and Fine-Grained Annotation Framework
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate through long-horizon trajectories involving user instructions, tool use, external observations, and memory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate behavioral outcomes but provide limited support for fine-grained attribution analysis. We introduce trajectory attribution and develop a benchmark and annotation framework for this task. The benchmark organizes heterogeneous trajectories under a unified component schema and provides annotations of the primary attribution component, together with attack and execution chains where applicable. Instantiating the benchmark with trajectories from AgentDojo and the Stage and Canary settings of Agent3Sigma yields more than 1,300 annotated trajectories covering task-aligned actions, unsafe actions, and safety refusals. The benchmark defines two evaluation tasks, primary attribution localization and attribution-chain recovery, and provides reference baselines based on incremental trajectory contribution and component-level leave-one-out perturbation. It captures diverse attribution settings, including local and long-range attribution as well as structured attribution chains. Reference baseline

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new benchmark and annotation framework to analyze the behavior of large language model (LLM) agents over long sequences of actions, called 'trajectories.' These trajectories include user instructions, tool use, external observations, and memory, and the framework helps identify which components are most responsible for the agent's final output or behavior.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals the growing complexity and autonomy of AI agents, which could disrupt digital markets by enabling new forms of competition or reinforcing existing gatekeepers' control over user interactions.
_analysis.market_signal: LLM agents with fine-grained attribution capabilities may reduce reliance on dominant platforms (e.g., search engines) by enabling more direct, tool-based user interactions.

items.title: Where Does AI Innovation Go? Measuring Research Attention Imbalance in AI Music
items.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in music has expanded research from generation and information retrieval to education, health, and governance. Yet this growth does not necessarily imply balanced research attention. Where is research attention directed across diverse music tasks, and how can such imbalance be systematically measured? Existing studies examine AI music from separate technical, application-specific, or bibliometric perspectives, but lack a systematic framework for measuring field-level imbalance. To address this gap, we analyze 6,839 AI music publications from 2015 to April 2026 using a joint taxonomy of 12 application categories and 11 technical method families. We propose the Research Attention Profile, comprising four indicators of technical investment, method allocation, methodological diversity, and frontier-method adoption lag. Results show that technical support is concentrated in scalable, content-oriented tasks, while education, health, and governance remain under-supported. Generation adopts frontier methods after only 0.33 years on average, compared with 4.33 years for education and 5.00 years for health. These findings reveal uneven methodo

_analysis.summary: This study examines whether research attention in AI-driven music innovation is evenly distributed across different music-related tasks (e.g., generation, education, health) or skewed toward certain areas. By analyzing 6,839 AI music publications, the authors develop a framework to measure field-level imbalances in research focus, revealing potential gaps in innovation priorities.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on research imbalances in AI music, it indirectly highlights how concentrated innovation in specific AI applications could lead to market power imbalances among firms specializing in those areas.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that AI innovation in music may become dominated by a few specialized firms, potentially creating winner-takes-all dynamics in niche AI markets.

items.title: Prune Once: Retraining-Free Task-Agnostic Pruning for Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable generalization across diverse multimodal tasks through large-scale pre-training, yet their rapidly increasing computational and memory requirements pose significant challenges for deployment in constrained environments. Existing pruning strategies often depend on task-specific criteria or LLM-oriented importance measures, making them unsuitable for task-agnostic pruning, where no task-specific samples are available at pruning time and the pruned model remains broadly applicable. We introduce a retraining-free VLM pruning framework called PORTA that derives a task- and modality-agnostic importance formulation based on activation variation, estimated from generic calibration data, which reliably captures feature-level representation utility across modalities. PORTA further incorporates an adaptive sparsity allocation mechanism that assigns layer-wise pruning ratios based on output feature variability, avoiding the limitations of uniform sparsity and reducing performance degradation at high compression levels. Extensive experiments across VLM architectures, such as CLIP, BLIP, and Qwen2-VL, demonstrate that PORTA achieves competit

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a new method called 'Prune Once' for reducing the size of vision-language models (VLMs) without needing to retrain them, making them more efficient for use in devices with limited computing power. VLMs are AI systems that understand both images and text, and this technique could make them more widely deployable without losing their ability to handle diverse tasks.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals how advances in AI efficiency could lower barriers to entry for smaller firms or open-source projects, potentially disrupting the dominance of large tech companies that control proprietary AI models.
_analysis.market_signal: Efficient AI models may enable new competitors to challenge established players in multimodal AI markets by reducing reliance on expensive cloud computing resources.

items.title: SkillEval: Decomposing Agent Skill Quality into Interpretable Signals
items.abstract: Agent skills provide reusable procedural knowledge that helps agents solve specialized tasks. As their use expands, evaluating skill quality becomes increasingly important. Existing evaluations often measure skill quality by testing whether a skill improves performance on specific downstream tasks. However, a reusable skill may apply to multiple task scenarios. Downstream evaluation mainly reflects the compatibility between a skill and the evaluated task, provides only a partial view of skill quality, and does not identify which aspect of the skill should be improved. We find that general properties of the \texttt{SKILL.md} document play an important role in skill quality. To evaluate these properties, we propose \textbf{SkillEval}, an interpretable framework for document-level skill evaluation. SkillEval evaluates each property using a fixed and inspectable scoring direction, producing interpretable scores. It further measures and reduces the influence of unrelated document features, such as length and formatting, so that each score captures its intended semantic property more specifically. Specifically, SkillEval learns an interpretable direction for each quality property from co

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces *SkillEval*, a method to evaluate the quality of reusable AI agent skills by breaking them down into interpretable signals rather than just testing their performance on specific tasks. The authors argue that current evaluations focus too narrowly on task compatibility, missing broader insights into skill quality that could help improve AI systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about competition policy, it highlights how AI agent capabilities could reshape digital markets by enabling more modular, reusable tools that reduce barriers to entry for competitors.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of reusable AI skills may lower switching costs for businesses adopting AI tools, potentially increasing competition in AI-driven markets.

items.title: Georeferencing Non-Gazetteered Place Names using Biological Specimen Records
items.abstract: Biological specimen records collected by natural history institutions constitute a rich source of temporal geographic knowledge, capturing biodiversity information about regional landscapes as they were recorded at different times. Using digitised data from the Allan Herbarium (New Zealand), this study identifies place names in these specimen locality descriptions that are absent from current gazetteers; we refer to these as non-gazetteer place names (NGPs). These place names are typically historical, vernacular, or colloquial and were used as landmarks to describe a specimen's location at the time of collection. We then investigate the problem of georeferencing the NGPs using only the limited information available in the specimen records. To resolve this, we leverage repeated occurrences of the same place name across specimen records with different specimen locations and spatial relation terms, extracting and inverting these relations to derive constraints on NGP locations. This approach is instantiated within deterministic, probabilistic, and LLM-based methods, enabling a comparative analysis of their strengths and limitations for text-based spatial inference. On a pseudo-NGP ben

_analysis.summary: This study uses digitised biological specimen records from the Allan Herbarium in New Zealand to identify place names (called 'non-gazetteer place names' or NGPs) that are missing from official geographic databases (gazetteers). These NGPs are often historical, local, or informal names used to describe locations in the past, revealing gaps in standardised geographic data.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this paper focuses on geographic data gaps in biodiversity records, it highlights the broader issue of fragmented and incomplete data ecosystems, which can affect digital platform competition in geospatial services.
_analysis.market_signal: The study signals the importance of high-quality, standardised geographic data for digital services, which is critical for location-based platforms and could influence competition in geospatial data markets.

items.title: SkillAligner: Treating Retrieved Skills as Adaptable Drafts at Execution Time
items.abstract: General-purpose skills promise reusable procedural knowledge for language agents, yet semantic relevance does not guarantee execution utility: a retrieved skill may encode assumptions that conflict with the current task, execution environment, or other retrieved skills. We formalize this problem as the skill--execution misfit. To address it, we propose SkillAligner, a training-free execution-time skill adaptation framework that treats retrieved skills as adaptable drafts rather than fixed instructions. Before execution, SkillAligner performs a one-time joint adaptation that specializes useful skill fragments to task requirements, aligns their procedural assumptions with the available execution interface, and composes the resulting guidance by resolving dependencies, conflicts, and redundancy across skills. The adapted content is consolidated into a compact execution guide and reused throughout the subsequent trajectory. Extensive experiments across diverse agent benchmarks and model backbones show that SkillAligner substantially improves task performance over existing skill-use baselines, reduces skill-induced regressions at the instance level, and lowers total inference cost.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces SkillAligner, a new method for improving how AI agents use 'skills' (reusable procedural knowledge) by adapting them to fit specific tasks and environments before execution. The authors argue that current AI systems struggle because skills may not work well together or match the task's needs, leading to 'skill--execution misfit.' SkillAligner addresses this by treating skills as flexible drafts that can be adjusted on-the-fly.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work signals how AI agents could become more capable and autonomous, potentially reducing reliance on dominant platforms (e.g., cloud providers or app ecosystems) by enabling customizable, interoperable skills.
_analysis.market_signal: AI agents with adaptive skills may disrupt platform-dependent markets by enabling more flexible, third-party solutions that bypass traditional gatekeepers.

items.title: Pessimal Elections for Approximately Dominating Sets
items.abstract: Condorcet's paradox is a foundational result in social choice theory, showing that no matter which candidate wins an election, a majority of voters may prefer some losing candidate. Worse still, even if the election can choose a committee of $k$ winners, some loser may beat every winner in a majority vote. Recent work showed that this obstruction can be sidestepped by relaxing the majority threshold. For all $\varepsilon > 0$, any election can select a committee of $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ winners such that no loser is preferred to every winner by $\frac12 + \varepsilon$ fraction of voters. We present a simple construction, found by GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, which proves that this result is tight up to a constant factor.

_analysis.summary: This paper explores Condorcet's paradox in social choice theory, where election winners can be beaten by losing candidates in majority votes. It shows that by relaxing the majority threshold slightly (e.g., requiring a 51% + ε majority instead of 50%), elections can select a small committee of winners (O(1/ε²)) such that no losing candidate is preferred by a majority of voters over every winner. This work is about designing fairer voting systems but has indirect implications for algorithmic decision-making in digital platforms.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital competition, the paper’s insights into majority thresholds and committee selection could inform discussions on algorithmic fairness or voting mechanisms in platform governance, which may intersect with competition policy in data-driven markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that small changes in majority thresholds (e.g., in recommendation systems or platform governance) can significantly alter outcomes, hinting at how digital platforms might design fairer algorithms without sacrificing efficiency.

items.title: CEDAR: Agent-Orchestrated Tree Search for Goal-Directed Optimization of Complex Systems
items.abstract: Complex systems, core objects of study in artificial life, model diverse phenomena through nonlinear, feedback-driven interactions that produce emergent behavior, with applications from population dynamics and biology to economic policy and strategic decision-making. Yet the difficulty of predicting how feedback structure gives rise to emergent behavior, a central open problem in artificial life, makes goal-directed design exceptionally challenging. In established practice, system structures are written in specialized modeling languages such as DYNAMO or STELLA, compounding the challenge with labor-intensive workflows that limit adoption and hinder timely decision-making. To address these challenges, we introduce CEDAR, an autonomous method that uses Large Language Model (LLM) agents to discover complex systems satisfying user-specified behavioral goals. Our key innovation is an LLM-driven Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) deeply coupled with complex systems: at each iteration, an LLM Judge evaluates emergent behavior against specified goals and an LLM Editor proposes improved variants, with the Judge acting as a fitness function and the Editor as a variation operator, akin to a gener

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces CEDAR, an AI system that uses agent-orchestrated tree search to optimize complex systems with nonlinear feedback loops, which are common in economics, biology, and strategic decision-making. The authors argue that predicting emergent behavior in such systems is difficult, making goal-directed design challenging.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: CEDAR's ability to model and optimize complex feedback-driven systems could enhance AI-driven strategic decision-making in digital markets, potentially altering competitive dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: AI systems capable of optimizing complex market interactions may enable new forms of algorithmic competition or strategic maneuvering by firms.

items.title: Multi-Agent Forensic Reasoning for Generalizable Deepfake Video Detection
items.abstract: The malicious use of generative artificial intelligence to create highly realistic deepfake videos raises serious ethical concerns and poses substantial challenges to AI safety. However, existing deepfake video benchmarks provide limited coverage of recent synthesis methods and generally lack reliable fine-grained textual annotations. Meanwhile, conventional detectors and multimodal large language models (MLLMs), whether operating as a single model or relying on a single analytical perspective, often fail to capture subtle forgery artifacts, limiting their generalization to emerging AI-generated methods. To address these limitations, we introduce FaceVid-Forensics-100K, a large-scale deepfake video dataset comprising 100,000 videos and spanning 33 synthesis methods across face swapping, face reenactment, and entire-face synthesis, including recent generators such as Seedance 2.0. The dataset provides fine-grained textual annotations of visual observations and verdict-consistent forensic explanations, automatically synthesized through a multi-model aggregation and conflict-resolution pipeline powered by advanced MLLMs. Building on this benchmark, we propose a multi-agent forensic re

_analysis.summary: This academic paper examines the challenge of detecting deepfake videos—hyper-realistic AI-generated videos used maliciously—highlighting that current detection methods and benchmarks are outdated and ineffective against newer AI synthesis techniques. It proposes a new approach called 'multi-agent forensic reasoning' to improve detection by analyzing videos from multiple perspectives, addressing the limitations of single-model or single-view detectors.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a shift in the AI arms race between generative AI creators and detection systems, which could disrupt market dynamics by enabling new players to challenge incumbent platform control over content moderation and authenticity verification.
_analysis.market_signal: The rise of advanced deepfake detection technologies may create new markets for authenticity verification services, potentially challenging the dominance of large platforms in content moderation and AI governance.

items.title: Gated-BEPO: Confidence-Gated Bellman Credit Assignment for Large Language Model Agents
items.abstract: Training large language model agents in long-horizon environments requires assigning credit from sparse terminal outcomes to individual actions. Existing critic-free methods propagate trajectory-level rewards uniformly across steps, while recent approaches construct step-level groups by matching repeated states and compare actions within each group. The former cannot distinguish useful actions in failed trajectories from ineffective actions in successful ones. The latter rely on step credit derived directly from individual trajectory outcomes and fixed-weight fusion with episode-level credit. We propose Gated-BEPO, which derives step-level credit from empirical rollout graphs. For each rollout group, Gated-BEPO constructs an empirical graph and estimates node values through a mean-backup Bellman fixed point that reflects the empirical action distribution of the current policy. We then accumulate these temporal-difference residuals along each sampled trajectory using generalized advantage estimation, yielding step-level Bellman advantages that capture both immediate and downstream effects. To adaptively fuse episode- and step-level credit, a confidence gate incorporates Bellman cred

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a new method called Gated-BEPO to improve how AI agents learn from long-term outcomes by better assigning credit to individual actions. Current methods either treat all steps equally or rely on fixed rules to distribute rewards, which can misidentify effective actions. The authors argue their approach helps agents distinguish useful actions in failed attempts from ineffective ones in successful ones.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work highlights how advances in AI agent training could enable more sophisticated autonomous systems that may disrupt digital markets by improving efficiency or enabling new business models.
_analysis.market_signal: Improved AI agent training could accelerate the deployment of autonomous systems in digital markets, potentially intensifying competition in sectors like e-commerce, cloud services, or digital advertising.

items.title: Autonomy-of-Heads: Data-Free Sparse Attention from Frozen Query-Key Geometry
items.abstract: Long-context LLM inference is bottlenecked by quadratic attention computation and growing KV-cache costs. Existing sparse attention and KV-compression methods typically decide which tokens or heads to preserve from runtime attention scores, observation windows, calibration prompts, or learned gates, making head diagnosis input-dependent and costly to deploy. We propose Autonomy-of-Heads (AoH), a data-free method that identifies retrieval and streaming heads from the spectral geometry of query-key projections. AoH defines the kernel attention operator $M_h = W_K^{h\top}W_Q^h$ and uses its effective-rank as a weight-space measure of head function: concentrated spectra indicate a small number of dominant query-key matching directions and are associated with retrieval heads, whereas diffuse spectra indicate the absence of a dominant global matching direction and are associated with streaming heads. We further derive an efficient $d_\text{head}$-dimensional computation that avoids constructing the full $d_\text{model}\times d_\text{model}$ matrix. We conducted extensive experiments across models demonstrating that at 50\% sparsity, AoH retains 96.5\% of Full Attention performance on ave

_analysis.summary: This academic paper proposes a new method called Autonomy-of-Heads (AoH) to improve the efficiency of large language models (LLMs) by reducing the computational cost of attention mechanisms—a key bottleneck in processing long-context inputs. The method identifies 'retrieval' and 'streaming' heads (specialized components of the model) without needing additional data, by analyzing the mathematical properties of query-key projections in the model's architecture.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper signals a potential reduction in barriers to entry for AI model providers by lowering computational costs, which could intensify competition in the LLM market by enabling smaller players to compete with large incumbents.
_analysis.market_signal: Efficient LLM architectures may democratize access to advanced AI, challenging the dominance of tech giants with proprietary, high-cost models.

items.title: Auction Design with a Bit of Information
items.abstract: Consider a revenue-maximizing seller who can access a binary signal about two bidders` joint values. We explore what kind of information is most valuable to the seller by studying three classes of signals, each capturing a distinct dimension of bidders` values: their overall level (demand), their relative strength (ranking), and their dispersion while preserving bidder anonymity (competitiveness). We characterize the optimal signal and corresponding auction mechanism within each class, and find that competitiveness signals are particularly effective. Under certain regularity conditions, the optimal competitiveness signal yields at least as much revenue as any ranking signal or demand signal. Moreover, for signals that induce a monotone allocation, the optimal competitiveness signal yields at least as much revenue as any other binary signal.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper studies how a seller can maximize revenue by using different types of information about two bidders' values in an auction. It compares three kinds of signals—overall demand, relative ranking, and competitiveness (how close the bidders' values are)—and finds that competitiveness signals are especially effective for boosting revenue under certain conditions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This paper provides insights into how information asymmetry and bidder competitiveness shape auction outcomes, which is relevant for understanding competitive dynamics in digital ad markets and platform-mediated auctions.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that fine-grained information about bidder competitiveness can significantly alter auction revenues, suggesting that digital platforms with access to such data may wield outsized market power.

items.title: Two Types of Tertiarization: Household Demand, Production Networks, and the Rise of Services
items.abstract: I measure whether the rise of services is ultimately supported by household consumption or by non-household demand through production networks, investment, exports, and government. Using harmonized input-output tables for 76 economies over 1995-2022, I attribute service value added to its ultimate domestic final-demand category and measure the household orientation of each service economy in both levels and growth. The conventional service share does not reveal the type: it is negatively correlated with household orientation, and only about four in ten tertiarization episodes are majority-household. Among the 65 economies whose service share rose over 1995-2018, 77 percent became less household-oriented; the share is 75 percent under a two-percentage-point material-change threshold. Yet household-supported production becomes more service-intensive with income because households' aggregate position falls faster. A one-type benchmark has no purchaser margin; a two-type extension gives the condition for this reversal. An exact Leontief accounting and Shapley decomposition allocate a median 73 percent of service-share growth to production-system channels, which are the largest contribu

_analysis.summary: This paper examines why economies are shifting toward services (a trend called 'tertiarization') by analyzing whether this shift is driven by household spending (like consumers buying services) or by non-household demand (like businesses using services in production or exports). Using data from 76 countries over 27 years, it finds that most service growth comes from non-household demand, and that the traditional measure of service share doesn’t reveal this breakdown—only about 40% of service expansions are mainly driven by households.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on broad economic trends in services, it indirectly highlights how digital services (a subset of services) may be driven by business-to-business demand rather than consumer demand, which could influence how regulators assess market power in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The dominance of non-household demand in service growth suggests that digital platform markets (where B2B services are critical) may be shaped more by enterprise adoption than consumer trends.

items.title: Capacity Markets for Large Loads under Supply-Chain Constraints
items.abstract: Motivated by the rapid growth of data centers, we develop a model to evaluate bringyour-own-capacity (BYOC) mandates and flexibility accreditation in capacity markets for new large loads with shared supply-chain constraints. With efficient pricing, BYOC mainly reallocates procurement between grid-built and self-built capacity and therefore has little welfare effect, while flexibility delivers a modest gain by reducing the effective capacity requirement. Under administrative price caps, mandates can improve static welfare by forcing data centers to internalize the full cost of capacity. The welfare ranking of the two instruments depends on supply-chain stress. At low or moderate stress, only the flexibility instrument raises welfare. Under severe stress with capped prices, the welfare gain from the BYOC obligation can exceed the gross flexibility benefit. The two instruments differ in their effects on a neighboring market: a unilateral BYOC mandate can crowd out its capacity investment, while flexibility produces essentially no spillover at our calibrated benchmark. Finally, applying current capacity non-performance penalties to flexible loads may lead to financial incentives that a

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how large electricity consumers like data centers could participate in capacity markets (mechanisms to ensure grid reliability) under supply-chain constraints. It finds that rules requiring data centers to build their own power capacity (BYOC) or prove flexibility in usage have limited overall welfare effects unless prices are artificially capped, in which case mandates can force these large loads to pay the true cost of capacity.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on electricity markets, the paper’s insights into supply-chain constraints and large-load procurement dynamics could indirectly inform debates about digital infrastructure bottlenecks and the market power of cloud providers.
_analysis.market_signal: Highlights the growing energy demands of data centers as a potential bottleneck in digital infrastructure, signaling the need for policy attention to energy market design in digital competition.

items.title: There Ain't No Such Thing as a Free Equilibrium
items.abstract: I argue that there is a sense in which universal equilibrium (defined loosely) existence in games is incompatible with eschewing strictly dominated strategies and a sense in which it isn't.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper explores the theoretical limits of universal equilibrium in game theory, arguing that strict adherence to equilibrium concepts may conflict with the elimination of strictly dominated strategies (a core principle in game theory where players avoid obviously bad moves). The paper suggests that in some cases, these two ideas cannot coexist, while in others, they can.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper is highly theoretical and does not directly address digital markets or competition policy, its discussion of equilibrium and strategic behavior could indirectly inform debates about market stability, platform strategies, or algorithmic decision-making in digital ecosystems.
_analysis.market_signal: This paper signals ongoing academic debate about the robustness of equilibrium-based models in complex systems, which could influence future research on digital platform dynamics or AI-driven market interactions.

items.title: Stochastic Choice with Distribution-Dependent Preferences
items.abstract: We develop a continuous-time stochastic choice theory with endogenous preference evolution. Unlike dynamic random utility, observed behavior affects future preferences through the conditional distribution of latent preference states, generating endogenous distributional feedback. We show that this feedback has observable behavioral implications and characterize stochastic choice by a behavioral representation consisting of contemporaneous choice and continuation behavior. This representation is identified from stochastic choice, yields a rigidity result linking structural preference dynamics to observable behavior, and characterizes exactly when distribution dependent utility is behaviorally reducible to dynamic random utility. We further prove a behavioral impossibility theorem: stochastic choice arrays exhibiting behavioral distributional feedback admit no dynamic random utility representation. On the probabilistic side, we establish existence and weak uniqueness for the underlying conditional McKean-Vlasov system with conditional law feedback. The structure unifies endogenous information, latent preference dynamics, behavioral identification, and stochastic choice within a singl

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new theory of how people make choices over time when their preferences aren’t fixed but evolve based on their past decisions. It shows that past behavior can shape future preferences through feedback loops, creating observable patterns in how people act. The authors develop a way to represent these choices mathematically, linking short-term decisions to long-term behavioral changes.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This research helps explain how digital platforms (like social media or recommendation systems) might influence user preferences over time, which is key to assessing their market power and potential for consumer harm.
